title: Q001 · Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
body: A 62-year-old man presents to nephrology with fatigue and reduced appetite. His past medical history includes hypertension. His current medications include amlodipine.
full:
A 62-year-old man presents to nephrology with fatigue and reduced appetite. His past medical history includes hypertension. His current medications include amlodipine.
Over the past three weeks, his kidney function has declined rapidly. His blood pressure is 152/90 mmHg, heart rate is 88 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.1 C. Serum creatinine is 3.6 mg/dL today. It was 1.1 mg/dL three weeks ago. Estimated glomerular filtration rate was 72 mL/min/1.73 m2 three weeks ago and is 18 mL/min/1.73 m2 today. Anti-proteinase 3 antibody testing is positive. History and investigations are not consistent with a secondary vasculitis.. Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood, 2+ protein, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.8 g/day.
Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
A. Repeat anti-proteinase 3 antibody testing before treatment and perform a kidney biopsy only if the antibody remains positive
B. Perform a kidney biopsy first and commence treatment only after histologic confirmation
C. Commence treatment now and perform a kidney biopsy soon after starting treatment when feasible
D. Commence treatment now and omit kidney biopsy because positive anti-proteinase 3 antibodies establish the diagnosis
E. Observe kidney function and perform a kidney biopsy only if the serum creatinine continues to increase
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: C. Commence treatment now and perform a kidney biopsy soon after starting treatment when feasible
PART C - Explanation
The key findings are a clinical presentation compatible with ANCA-associated kidney vasculitis, positive anti-proteinase 3 antibodies, low suspicion for secondary vasculitis, and rapidly progressive loss of kidney function. Serum creatinine increased from 1.1 mg/dL to 3.6 mg/dL over three weeks, accompanied by dysmorphic hematuria, red blood cell casts, and moderate proteinuria.
According to KDIGO, when a patient has a compatible clinical presentation, positive proteinase 3 ANCA or myeloperoxidase ANCA, low suspicion for secondary vasculitis, and rapidly progressive disease at an experienced center, treatment should be commenced without waiting for kidney biopsy. Kidney biopsy should be considered after treatment has started if feasible. This approach allows treatment to begin promptly in rapidly progressive disease while still obtaining a kidney biopsy when feasible.

title: Q002 · Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic investigation?
body: A 60-year-old man presents to nephrology with fatigue and a new purpuric rash over the lower limbs. His past medical history includes hypertension. His current medications include amlodipine.
full:
A 60-year-old man presents to nephrology with fatigue and a new purpuric rash over the lower limbs. His past medical history includes hypertension. His current medications include amlodipine.
Two weeks ago, blood tests showed a serum creatinine of 1.1 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 77 mL/min/1.73 m2. His blood pressure today is 148/86 mmHg, heart rate is 84 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.0 C. Blood tests now show a serum creatinine of 3.2 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 21 mL/min/1.73 m2. Anti-proteinase 3 antibody and anti-myeloperoxidase antibody testing by antigen-specific immunoassays are negative.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood, 2+ protein, 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.7 g/day.
Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic investigation?
A. Complete blood count
B. Repeat anti-proteinase 3 and anti-myeloperoxidase antibody testing
C. C-reactive protein measurement
D. Kidney biopsy
E. Serum complement C3 and C4 measurement
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: D. Kidney biopsy
PART C - Explanation
The key finding is the rapid numerical decline in kidney function together with an active glomerular urine sediment and moderate proteinuria. Serum creatinine has increased from 1.1 mg/dL to 3.2 mg/dL over two weeks, while the estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 77 to 21 mL/min/1.73 m2. These findings are compatible with necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis in the appropriate clinical setting.
According to KDIGO, approximately 90% of patients with small-vessel vasculitis or necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis have ANCA directed mainly against myeloperoxidase or proteinase 3, but negative ANCA testing does not exclude the diagnosis. When the clinical presentation is compatible with a primary small-vessel vasculitis, both proteinase 3 ANCA and myeloperoxidase ANCA are negative, and there is no contraindication to biopsy, kidney biopsy is the appropriate next diagnostic investigation.

title: Q003 · Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?
body: A 29-year-old man presents with a 10-day history of fatigue and cough. Over the past 5 days, he has developed progressive shortness of breath and recurrent blood-streaked sputum. During the past 3 day
full:
A 29-year-old man presents with a 10-day history of fatigue and cough. Over the past 5 days, he has developed progressive shortness of breath and recurrent blood-streaked sputum. During the past 3 days, he has also noticed dark-colored urine and reduced urine output. He has no known history of kidney disease. His current medications include no prescription medications.
Two weeks ago, during a routine health examination, his serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 112 mL/min/1.73 m2. His blood pressure today is 146/88 mmHg, heart rate is 102 beats per minute, temperature is 37.1 C, and oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. Blood tests now show a serum creatinine of 3.8 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 19 mL/min/1.73 m2. Chest imaging demonstrates bilateral pulmonary infiltrates compatible with alveolar hemorrhage. Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody testing is positive. Anti-proteinase 3 antibody and anti-myeloperoxidase antibody testing are negative.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood, 2+ protein, 40 to 50 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.8 g/day.
Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?
A. Provide supportive care while awaiting kidney biopsy and begin plasma exchange only if the biopsy confirms the diagnosis
B. Begin urgent plasma exchange without waiting for diagnostic kidney biopsy
C. Repeat anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody testing before deciding whether to begin plasma exchange
D. Monitor kidney function and pulmonary findings for several days before considering plasma exchange
E. Defer plasma exchange unless kidney function continues to decline despite supportive care
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: B. Begin urgent plasma exchange without waiting for diagnostic kidney biopsy
PART C - Explanation

The patient has a pulmonary–renal syndrome characterized by alveolar hemorrhage, hypoxemia, rapidly declining kidney function, hematuria, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. His serum creatinine has increased from 0.9 mg/dL to 3.8 mg/dL over two weeks, while his estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 112 to 19 mL/min/1.73 m2.
 According to KDIGO, simultaneous pulmonary and kidney injury should raise concern for a vasculitic or anti-glomerular basement membrane process, and serologic testing is particularly important in this setting. A positive anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody test suggests anti-glomerular basement membrane disease and indicates the need for urgent plasma exchange without waiting for a positive diagnostic kidney biopsy.
More generally, KDIGO identifies several situations in which plasma exchange should be considered in ANCA-associated vasculitis, including a serum creatinine greater than 3.4 mg/dL, requirement for dialysis, rapidly increasing serum creatinine, or diffuse alveolar hemorrhage with hypoxemia. Plasma exchange should also be added in patients with overlap between ANCA-associated vasculitis and anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, and it can be considered in refractory disease.

title: Q004 · Which of the following serologic testing strategies is most appropriate at this time?
body: A 36-year-old man presents with a 9-day history of fatigue and cough. Over the past 4 days, he has developed increasing shortness of breath and several episodes of blood-streaked sputum. He has no kno
full:
A 36-year-old man presents with a 9-day history of fatigue and cough. Over the past 4 days, he has developed increasing shortness of breath and several episodes of blood-streaked sputum. He has no known history of kidney disease. His current medications include no prescription medications.
Twelve days ago, his serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 109 mL/min/1.73 m2. His blood pressure today is 144/86 mmHg, heart rate is 102 beats per minute, temperature is 37.2 C, and oxygen saturation is 89% on room air. Blood tests now show a serum creatinine of 3.4 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 22 mL/min/1.73 m2. Chest imaging demonstrates bilateral diffuse pulmonary infiltrates.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood, 2+ protein, 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.9 g/day.
Which of the following serologic testing strategies is most appropriate at this time?
A. Test for proteinase 3 ANCA and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies without myeloperoxidase ANCA testing
B. Test for myeloperoxidase ANCA and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies without proteinase 3 ANCA testing
C. Test for myeloperoxidase ANCA and proteinase 3 ANCA using antigen-specific immunoassays, together with anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies
D. Test for myeloperoxidase ANCA and proteinase 3 ANCA without anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody testing
E. Test for anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies without myeloperoxidase ANCA or proteinase 3 ANCA testing
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: C. Test for myeloperoxidase ANCA and proteinase 3 ANCA using antigen-specific immunoassays, together with anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies
PART C - Explanation
The patient has concurrent pulmonary and glomerular kidney findings. He has blood-streaked sputum, hypoxemia, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates together with a rapid decline in kidney function. His serum creatinine has increased from 0.9 mg/dL to 3.4 mg/dL over 12 days, while his estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 109 to 22 mL/min/1.73 m2. Dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts further indicate glomerular kidney injury.
According to KDIGO, simultaneous lung and kidney injury should raise concern for vasculitis, and serologic testing is of major diagnostic importance. A positive myeloperoxidase ANCA or proteinase 3 ANCA supports ANCA-associated vasculitis, whereas a positive anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody test suggests anti-glomerular basement membrane disease. High-quality antigen-specific immunoassays are the preferred screening method for myeloperoxidase ANCA and proteinase 3 ANCA.

title: Q005 · Which of the following best describes the kidney lesion in this patient?
body: A 52-year-old woman presents with fatigue, nasal congestion, and reduced appetite. Her past medical history includes hypertension. Her current medications include amlodipine.
full:
A 52-year-old woman presents with fatigue, nasal congestion, and reduced appetite. Her past medical history includes hypertension. Her current medications include amlodipine.
Two weeks ago, serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 67 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure today is 150/88 mmHg, heart rate is 92 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.3 C. Blood tests now show a serum creatinine of 3.1 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 17 mL/min/1.73 m2. Anti-proteinase 3 antibody testing is positive.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood, 2+ protein, 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 2.1 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 18 glomeruli, with segmental fibrinoid necrosis in 5 glomeruli and cellular crescents in 7 glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
Which of the following best describes the kidney lesion in this patient?
A. Anti-glomerular basement membrane crescentic glomerulonephritis
B. Pauci-immune focal and segmental necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis
C. Immune-complex necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis
D. Immunoglobulin A nephropathy with crescent formation
E. C3-dominant glomerulonephritis with crescent formation
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: B. Pauci-immune focal and segmental necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis
PART C - Explanation
The patient has rapidly progressive glomerular kidney injury. Serum creatinine has increased from 1.0 mg/dL to 3.1 mg/dL over two weeks, with a decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate from 67 to 17 mL/min/1.73 m2. The urine sediment demonstrates microscopic hematuria, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts, while proteinuria is moderate at 2.1 g/day. Positive proteinase 3 ANCA further supports an ANCA-associated vasculitic process in this clinical setting.
The characteristic kidney lesion associated with ANCA-associated vasculitis is pauci-immune focal and segmental necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis. In this patient, light microscopy demonstrates focal segmental fibrinoid necrosis and cellular crescents, while immunofluorescence shows little or no immune deposition and electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense deposits. Together, these findings establish the pauci-immune pattern.

title: Q006 · Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of the negative anti-proteinase 3 and anti-myeloperoxidase antibody results?
body: A 57-year-old woman presents with fatigue, nasal congestion, and a new purpuric rash over the lower limbs. Her past medical history includes hypertension. Her current medications include amlodipine.
full:
A 57-year-old woman presents with fatigue, nasal congestion, and a new purpuric rash over the lower limbs. Her past medical history includes hypertension. Her current medications include amlodipine.
Three weeks ago, her serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 74 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure today is 148/88 mmHg, heart rate is 90 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.2 C. Blood tests now show a serum creatinine of 3.0 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 18 mL/min/1.73 m2. Anti-proteinase 3 antibody and anti-myeloperoxidase antibody testing by antigen-specific immunoassays are negative.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood, 2+ protein, 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.8 g/day.
Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of the negative anti-proteinase 3 and anti-myeloperoxidase antibody results?
A. The negative antibody results establish an immune-complex glomerulonephritis as the most likely cause of the kidney findings
B. ANCA-associated vasculitis is excluded because both major antigen-specific antibody tests are negative
C. Pauci-immune necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis is excluded because ANCA must be detectable when kidney involvement is present
D. The negative antibody results indicate that the decline in kidney function is unlikely to result from small-vessel vasculitis
E. ANCA-associated vasculitis remains a possible diagnosis despite negative serologic testing
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. ANCA-associated vasculitis remains a possible diagnosis despite negative serologic testing
PART C - Explanation
The patient has a clinical presentation compatible with small-vessel vasculitis involving the kidney. Her serum creatinine has increased from 0.9 mg/dL to 3.0 mg/dL over three weeks, while her estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 74 to 18 mL/min/1.73 m2. The urine sediment demonstrates glomerular hematuria with dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts, together with moderate proteinuria.
According to KDIGO, approximately 90% of patients with small-vessel vasculitis or necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis have ANCA, directed primarily against myeloperoxidase or proteinase 3. However, ANCA negativity does not exclude the diagnosis. The negative anti-proteinase 3 and anti-myeloperoxidase antibody results therefore reduce the serologic support for ANCA-associated vasculitis but do not eliminate it when the clinical presentation remains compatible.

title: Q007 · Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of the positive anti-proteinase 3 antibody result?
body: A 58-year-old woman is referred to nephrology after anti-proteinase 3 antibody testing obtained during an evaluation for several weeks of fatigue returns positive. Her past medical history includes hy
full:
A 58-year-old woman is referred to nephrology after anti-proteinase 3 antibody testing obtained during an evaluation for several weeks of fatigue returns positive. Her past medical history includes hypertension. Her current medications include amlodipine.
Her blood pressure is 142/84 mmHg, heart rate is 80 beats per minute, and temperature is 36.9 C. Serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 76 mL/min/1.73 m2, unchanged from measurements three months earlier. Complete blood count shows a hemoglobin level of 13.1 g/dL, white blood cell count of 6,800 cells per microliter, and platelet count of 248,000 cells per microliter. C-reactive protein is 3 mg/L. She reports no hemoptysis, shortness of breath, purpuric skin lesions, visual symptoms, or neurologic symptoms. Chest imaging shows no pulmonary infiltrates.
Urinalysis demonstrates no blood, trace protein, 0 to 2 red blood cells per high-power field, and no red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 0.1 g/day.
Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of the positive anti-proteinase 3 antibody result?
A. The result should be disregarded because ANCA testing has diagnostic value only when kidney dysfunction is already present
B. The result establishes ANCA-associated vasculitis regardless of the absence of compatible clinical manifestations
C. The result establishes granulomatosis with polyangiitis because proteinase 3 ANCA is positive
D. The result establishes active kidney vasculitis despite the normal kidney function and urine sediment
E. The result supports ANCA-associated vasculitis but must be interpreted together with the patient’s clinical findings, imaging, and other laboratory results
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. The result supports ANCA-associated vasculitis but must be interpreted together with the patient’s clinical findings, imaging, and other laboratory results
PART C - Explanation
A positive proteinase 3 ANCA can support a diagnosis of ANCA-associated vasculitis, but it does not establish the diagnosis by itself. In this patient, kidney function is stable, the urine sediment does not show glomerular hematuria or red blood cell casts, quantified proteinuria is minimal, chest imaging is unremarkable, and there are no clear extrarenal manifestations of small-vessel vasculitis.
According to KDIGO, the diagnosis of ANCA-associated vasculitis relies on the combination of clinical findings and the results of imaging studies and laboratory tests. Relevant laboratory assessment may include C-reactive protein, complete blood count, kidney parameters, urine sediment analysis, and antigen-specific testing for myeloperoxidase ANCA and proteinase 3 ANCA. A positive proteinase 3 ANCA result therefore provides diagnostic support only when interpreted within the overall clinical context.

title: Q008 · Which of the following is the preferred initial ANCA screening strategy in this patient?
body: A 46-year-old woman presents with fatigue, nasal congestion, and a persistent cough. Her past medical history includes hypertension. Her current medications include amlodipine.
full:
A 46-year-old woman presents with fatigue, nasal congestion, and a persistent cough. Her past medical history includes hypertension. Her current medications include amlodipine.
Three weeks ago, her serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 78 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure today is 148/86 mmHg, heart rate is 90 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.2 C. Blood tests now show a serum creatinine of 2.8 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 20 mL/min/1.73 m2. The combination of upper respiratory symptoms and rapidly declining kidney function raises concern for a small-vessel vasculitic process.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood, 2+ protein, 25 to 35 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.6 g/day.
Which of the following is the preferred initial ANCA screening strategy in this patient?
A. Anti-myeloperoxidase antibody testing alone because kidney involvement is present
B. Indirect immunofluorescence for ANCA alone without antigen-specific testing
C. Indirect immunofluorescence first, with myeloperoxidase and proteinase 3 antigen-specific testing only if the initial result is positive
D. Anti-proteinase 3 antibody testing alone because upper respiratory manifestations are present
E. High-quality antigen-specific immunoassays for myeloperoxidase ANCA and proteinase 3 ANCA
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. High-quality antigen-specific immunoassays for myeloperoxidase ANCA and proteinase 3 ANCA
PART C - Explanation
The patient has findings that warrant evaluation for ANCA-associated vasculitis, including upper respiratory manifestations, a rapid numerical decline in kidney function, microscopic hematuria with dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts, and moderate proteinuria. Her serum creatinine has increased from 0.9 mg/dL to 2.8 mg/dL over three weeks, while her estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 78 to 20 mL/min/1.73 m2.
According to the revised international consensus cited by KDIGO, high-quality antigen-specific immunoassays are the preferred screening method for myeloperoxidase ANCA and proteinase 3 ANCA in patients being evaluated for granulomatosis with polyangiitis or microscopic polyangiitis.

title: Q009 · Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic approach at this time?
body: A 63-year-old woman presents with fatigue, reduced appetite, and aching in both knees and ankles. Her past medical history includes hypertension. Her current medications include amlodipine.
full:
A 63-year-old woman presents with fatigue, reduced appetite, and aching in both knees and ankles. Her past medical history includes hypertension. Her current medications include amlodipine.
Two weeks ago, her serum creatinine was 0.8 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 84 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure today is 152/88 mmHg, heart rate is 94 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.3 C. Blood tests now show a serum creatinine of 3.0 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 17 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Urine dipstick demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein. Urine microscopy shows 35 to 45 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, red blood cell casts, and 8 to 10 white blood cells per high-power field. Urine culture shows no bacterial growth. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.9 g/day.
Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic approach at this time?
A. Obtain ANCA testing alone and proceed with further evaluation only if positive
B. Evaluate primarily for a nonglomerular cause of acute kidney injury because the rise in serum creatinine is the dominant abnormality
C. Repeat serum creatinine and urinalysis after several days before pursuing further diagnostic testing
D. Evaluate for possible glomerular disease by obtaining autoimmune serologies, assess for systemic features, exclude infection, and consider kidney biopsy if appropriate
E. Obtain kidney imaging to evaluate for urinary tract obstruction before any further workup
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: D. Evaluate for possible glomerular disease by obtaining autoimmune serologies, assess for systemic features, exclude infection, and consider kidney biopsy if appropriate
PART C - Explanation
The patient has a rapid decline in kidney function over a short period, with serum creatinine rising from 0.8 mg/dL to 3.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate falling from 84 to 17 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis shows hematuria and proteinuria, and urine microscopy demonstrates dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts, which are characteristic of glomerular injury. The presence of pyuria with a negative urine culture further supports a noninfectious inflammatory renal process.
This pattern is most consistent with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. The appropriate diagnostic approach is a broad evaluation for immune-mediated glomerular disease, including serologic testing (ANCA, anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies, antinuclear antibodies, and complement levels), assessment for systemic manifestations, exclusion of infection, and kidney biopsy when feasible.

title: Q010 · Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic direction at this time?
body: A 67-year-old man presents with fatigue, reduced appetite, and decreased urine output. His past medical history includes hypertension. His current medications include amlodipine.
full:
A 67-year-old man presents with fatigue, reduced appetite, and decreased urine output. His past medical history includes hypertension. His current medications include amlodipine.
Six days ago, his serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 79 mL/min/1.73 m2. His blood pressure today is 138/82 mmHg, heart rate is 88 beats per minute, and temperature is 36.9 C. Blood tests now show a serum creatinine of 3.1 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 20 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Urine dipstick shows no blood and trace protein. Urine microscopy demonstrates 0 to 2 red blood cells per high-power field, no dysmorphic red blood cells, no red blood cell casts, and 1 to 2 white blood cells per high-power field. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 0.1 g/day.
Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic direction at this time?
A. Evaluate specifically for ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis despite the absence of glomerular urine findings
B. Evaluate for rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with autoimmune serologies and kidney biopsy
C. Evaluate for a nonglomerular cause of acute kidney injury
D. Evaluate for anti-glomerular basement membrane disease as the primary explanation for the kidney dysfunction
E. Evaluate for immune-complex glomerulonephritis based on the rapid decline in kidney function alone
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: C. Evaluate for a nonglomerular cause of acute kidney injury
PART C - Explanation
The patient has developed a substantial decline in kidney function over six days, with serum creatinine increasing from 1.0 mg/dL to 3.1 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate falling from 79 to 20 mL/min/1.73 m2. However, the urine findings do not indicate a glomerular process. The dipstick shows no blood and only trace protein, while microscopy shows no glomerular hematuria, dysmorphic red blood cells, red blood cell casts, or pyuria.
The diagnostic strategy in KDIGO distinguishes rapid kidney-function decline accompanied by glomerular urine abnormalities from rapid kidney-function decline without those abnormalities. When blood and protein are not present in the expected glomerular pattern, or when the urine sediment does not demonstrate glomerular hematuria or pyuria without infection, the appropriate direction is to evaluate for a nonglomerular cause of acute kidney injury.

title: Q011 · Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of the persistent urinary abnormalities?
body: A 61-year-old woman with previously active myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis and kidney involvement returns for follow-up after completing induction therapy. At diagnosis four months ago, her
full:
A 61-year-old woman with previously active myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis and kidney involvement returns for follow-up after completing induction therapy. At diagnosis four months ago, her serum creatinine was 3.6 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 14 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis at that time demonstrated 3+ blood, 2+ protein, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. Proteinuria was 2.3 g/day.
She now reports no fatigue, respiratory symptoms, skin lesions, visual symptoms, or neurologic symptoms. Her blood pressure is 136/82 mmHg, heart rate is 78 beats per minute, and temperature is 36.8 C. Serum creatinine is 1.5 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 41 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score is 0.
Urinalysis still demonstrates 1+ blood and 1+ protein, with 8 to 12 red blood cells per high-power field. No red blood cell casts are identified. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 0.6 g/day.
Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of the persistent urinary abnormalities?
A. The patient cannot be considered in remission until both hematuria and proteinuria have completely resolved
B. The patient has active kidney vasculitis because any persistent microscopic hematuria after treatment indicates ongoing glomerulonephritis
C. The patient has experienced a kidney relapse because proteinuria remains detectable after induction therapy
D. The patient has treatment-resistant disease because hematuria and proteinuria have not completely disappeared
E. The patient may remain in remission because persistent hematuria and proteinuria do not necessarily indicate active vasculitis 
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. The patient may remain in remission because persistent hematuria and proteinuria do not necessarily indicate active vasculitis 
PART C - Explanation
The patient has improved substantially since treatment. Serum creatinine has fallen from 3.6 mg/dL to 1.5 mg/dL, estimated glomerular filtration rate has improved from 14 to 41 mL/min/1.73 m2, systemic manifestations are absent, and the Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score is 0. Although microscopic hematuria and proteinuria persist, both have decreased from their levels during active disease.
According to KDIGO, remission is characterized by the absence of manifestations of vasculitis and glomerulonephritis, with a Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score of 0. For glomerulonephritis, kidney function should be stable or improved. Hematuria and proteinuria can persist after active disease has resolved, and their persistence does not necessarily indicate ongoing disease activity.

title: Q012 · Which of the following best describes the patient’s current disease state?
body: A 59-year-old woman with myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis was diagnosed seven months ago after presenting with fatigue, microscopic hematuria, and rapidly declining kidney function. At diagn
full:
A 59-year-old woman with myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis was diagnosed seven months ago after presenting with fatigue, microscopic hematuria, and rapidly declining kidney function. At diagnosis, her serum creatinine was 3.5 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 15 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis demonstrated 3+ blood, 2+ protein, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimated proteinuria of 2.1 g/day. Kidney biopsy showed pauci-immune necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis. She received induction therapy.
Three months after starting treatment, her constitutional symptoms had resolved and she reported feeling well. Her Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score was 0. Serum creatinine had improved to 1.4 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate to 44 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis still showed 1+ blood and 1+ protein, with 5 to 8 red blood cells per high-power field and no red blood cell casts. Proteinuria was 0.4 g/day. These findings remained stable at her next follow-up visit.
Four months later, she returns with a two-week history of fatigue and dark-colored urine. Her blood pressure is 146/88 mmHg, heart rate is 88 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.1 C. Serum creatinine is now 2.2 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 27 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 35 to 45 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.6 g/day.
Which of the following best describes the patient’s current disease state?
A. Treatment-resistant kidney vasculitis that never achieved an initial remission
B. Persistent urinary abnormalities compatible with continued clinical remission
C. Kidney relapse occurring after a previously documented period of remission
D. Stable chronic kidney injury remaining after the previous vasculitic episode
E. Continued remission with fluctuating urinary findings but no renewed kidney activity
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: C. Kidney relapse occurring after a previously documented period of remission
PART C - Explanation
This patient had previously achieved remission after treatment. Her systemic symptoms resolved, her Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score was 0, kidney function improved substantially, and the remaining low-level hematuria and proteinuria were stable. Persistent hematuria or proteinuria during remission does not necessarily indicate ongoing active vasculitis.
The current presentation is different. Hematuria has increased from 1+ to 3+, proteinuria has increased from 0.4 g/day to 1.6 g/day, red blood cell casts have reappeared, and estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 44 to 27 mL/min/1.73 m2. According to KDIGO, relapse refers to increased disease activity after partial or complete remission, and a return or increase of hematuria together with proteinuria may indicate kidney relapse.

title: Q013 · Which of the following best describes the patient’s current disease state?
body: A 62-year-old man with proteinase 3 ANCA-associated vasculitis and kidney involvement was diagnosed four months ago after presenting with fatigue, nasal congestion, microscopic hematuria, and declinin
full:
A 62-year-old man with proteinase 3 ANCA-associated vasculitis and kidney involvement was diagnosed four months ago after presenting with fatigue, nasal congestion, microscopic hematuria, and declining kidney function. At diagnosis, his serum creatinine was 3.2 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 18 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis demonstrated 3+ blood, 2+ protein, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimated proteinuria of 2.0 g/day. He subsequently received induction therapy.
At follow-up, he reports that his fatigue and nasal symptoms have resolved. He has no cough, hemoptysis, skin lesions, visual symptoms, or neurologic symptoms. His blood pressure is 136/80 mmHg, heart rate is 76 beats per minute, and temperature is 36.8 C. His Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score is 0. Serum creatinine is now 1.5 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 43 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Urinalysis demonstrates 1+ blood and trace protein, with 4 to 6 red blood cells per high-power field and no red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 0.4 g/day.
Which of the following best describes the patient’s current disease state?
A. Persistent systemic vasculitis with residual kidney injury despite improvement after treatment
B. Kidney relapse with renewed glomerular activity despite improvement in systemic manifestations
C. Treatment-resistant vasculitis with persistent kidney involvement despite induction therapy
D. Ongoing active glomerulonephritis with incomplete response despite improvement in kidney function
E. Clinical remission with residual low-level urinary abnormalities after treated kidney vasculitis
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. Clinical remission with residual low-level urinary abnormalities after treated kidney vasculitis
PART C - Explanation
The patient has improved substantially after treatment. His systemic manifestations have resolved, his Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score is 0, serum creatinine has improved from 3.2 mg/dL to 1.5 mg/dL, and estimated glomerular filtration rate has improved from 21 to 52 mL/min/1.73 m2.
According to KDIGO, remission is characterized by the absence of manifestations of vasculitis and glomerulonephritis with a Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score of 0. In patients with glomerulonephritis, kidney function should be stable or improved. Importantly, persistent hematuria or proteinuria does not necessarily indicate ongoing active disease.

title: Q014 · The patient is initially assessed at a hospital that can provide general medical and nephrology care but has limited experience managing ANCA-associated vasculitis. Which of the following plans best addresses the next phase of this patient’s care?
body: A 48-year-old man presents with a 12-day history of fatigue, nasal congestion, and cough. During the past 3 days, he has developed increasing shortness of breath and several episodes of blood-streaked
full:
A 48-year-old man presents with a 12-day history of fatigue, nasal congestion, and cough. During the past 3 days, he has developed increasing shortness of breath and several episodes of blood-streaked sputum. He has no known history of kidney disease. His current medications include amlodipine for hypertension.
Three weeks ago, his serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 86 mL/min/1.73 m2. His blood pressure today is 154/90 mmHg, heart rate is 104 beats per minute, temperature is 37.2 C, and oxygen saturation is 89% on room air. Serum creatinine is now 4.1 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 17 mL/min/1.73 m2. Chest imaging demonstrates bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. Proteinase 3 ANCA testing is positive.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 40 to 50 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 2.0 g/day.
The patient is initially assessed at a hospital that can provide general medical and nephrology care but has limited experience managing ANCA-associated vasculitis. Which of the following plans best addresses the next phase of this patient’s care?
A. Arrange management at a center with AAV expertise, appropriate serologic and histologic testing, treatment modalities, intensive care, and acute hemodialysis
B. Transfer to a respiratory referral unit with intensive care access
C. Continue treatment locally with general nephrology support and arrange transfer only if kidney replacement therapy becomes necessary
D. Continue local stabilization while sending diagnostic samples and reconsider referral only if pulmonary or kidney abnormalities continue to progress
E. Arrange transfer to a tertiary nephrology center with kidney biopsy, intensive care, and acute hemodialysis capability
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: A. Arrange management at a center with AAV expertise, appropriate serologic and histologic testing, treatment modalities, intensive care, and acute hemodialysis
PART C - Explanation
The patient has a clinical presentation consistent with ANCA-associated vasculitis involving both the kidneys and lungs. His serum creatinine has increased from 1.0 mg/dL to 4.1 mg/dL over three weeks, estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 86 to 17 mL/min/1.73 m2, and the urine sediment demonstrates dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts. He also has hypoxemia and pulmonary infiltrates.
According to KDIGO Practice Point 9.1.2, patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis should be treated at centers experienced in AAV management. Such centers should have facilities for rapid diagnosis, including appropriate serologic and histologic testing, access to treatment modalities including rituximab and plasma exchange, experience with treatment-related complications, intensive care capability, and acute hemodialysis facilities.

title: Q015 · The patient and her family are concerned that her age may make disease-directed treatment more harmful than beneficial. Which of the following best reflects the prognostic evidence relevant to this decision?
body: A 79-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of fatigue, reduced appetite, arthralgia, and a new purpuric rash over both lower limbs. She has no previous history of vasculitis or chronic kidney
full:
A 79-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of fatigue, reduced appetite, arthralgia, and a new purpuric rash over both lower limbs. She has no previous history of vasculitis or chronic kidney disease. Her current medications include amlodipine for hypertension.
Three weeks ago, her serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 58 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure today is 150/86 mmHg, heart rate is 92 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.1 C. Serum creatinine is now 3.2 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 14 mL/min/1.73 m2. Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing is positive.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.8 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows focal segmental fibrinoid necrosis and cellular crescents. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
The patient and her family are concerned that her age may make disease-directed treatment more harmful than beneficial. Which of the following best reflects the prognostic evidence relevant to this decision?
A. Immunosuppressive treatment should be deferred until kidney function stabilizes because its survival benefit in older adults depends on spontaneous recovery of glomerular filtration
B. Supportive care alone is preferred because age older than 75 years outweighs the potential survival benefit of immunosuppressive treatment in patients with active systemic AAV
C. Immunosuppressive treatment remains appropriate because active systemic AAV has poor outcomes without therapy, and treatment has been associated with improved survival even in adults older than 75 years
D. Immunosuppressive treatment should be reserved for patients without kidney involvement because impaired kidney function at diagnosis indicates limited treatment benefit in older adults
E. Supportive care should be continued unless pulmonary hemorrhage develops because advanced age limits the survival benefit of immunosuppression when AAV primarily involves the kidneys
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: C. Immunosuppressive treatment remains appropriate because active systemic AAV has poor outcomes without therapy, and treatment has been associated with improved survival even in adults older than 75 years
PART C - Explanation
The patient has newly diagnosed active systemic ANCA-associated vasculitis with kidney involvement. Her serum creatinine has increased from 1.0 mg/dL to 3.2 mg/dL over three weeks, estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 58 to 14 mL/min/1.73 m2, the urine sediment demonstrates glomerular hematuria and red blood cell casts, and kidney biopsy shows pauci-immune necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis.
KDIGO identifies age and kidney function or kidney involvement at diagnosis as important factors associated with survival in AAV. However, advanced age does not make immunosuppressive treatment futile. Without immunosuppressive therapy, AAV is associated with poor outcomes, and immunosuppression is pivotal to improving survival in active systemic disease. This applies even to adults older than 75 years, in whom immunosuppressive treatment has been associated with improved survival.

title: Q016 · The patient and his family ask which features present at diagnosis are particularly important when considering his overall prognosis. Which of the following combinations is specifically identified as important for overall survival in ANCA-associated vasculitis?
body: A 72-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, reduced appetite, arthralgia, and a purpuric rash over both lower limbs. He has no previous history of vasculitis. His past medical history
full:
A 72-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, reduced appetite, arthralgia, and a purpuric rash over both lower limbs. He has no previous history of vasculitis. His past medical history includes hypertension, and his current medications include amlodipine.
One month ago, his serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 78 mL/min/1.73 m2. His blood pressure today is 148/86 mmHg, heart rate is 90 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.1 C. Serum creatinine is now 3.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 22 mL/min/1.73 m2. Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing is positive.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 25 to 35 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.7 g/day. Kidney biopsy confirms pauci-immune necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis.
The patient and his family ask which features present at diagnosis are particularly important when considering his overall prognosis. Which of the following combinations is specifically identified as important for overall survival in ANCA-associated vasculitis?
A. Duration of constitutional symptoms together with the amount of proteinuria at diagnosis
B. ANCA antigen specificity together with the degree of microscopic hematuria at diagnosis
C. Patient age together with kidney function or kidney involvement at diagnosis
D. Presence of cutaneous disease together with the degree of systemic inflammation at diagnosis
E. Presence of arthralgia together with the duration of symptoms before diagnosis
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: C. Patient age together with kidney function or kidney involvement at diagnosis
PART C - Explanation
The patient has newly diagnosed ANCA-associated vasculitis with substantial kidney involvement. His serum creatinine has increased from 1.0 mg/dL to 3.0 mg/dL, estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 78 to 22 mL/min/1.73 m2, and kidney biopsy confirms pauci-immune necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis.
KDIGO identifies age and kidney function and/or kidney involvement at diagnosis as important factors associated with survival in ANCA-associated vasculitis. These baseline characteristics should therefore be considered when discussing overall prognosis with a newly diagnosed patient.

title: Q017 · Because of the extensive chronic damage on biopsy, the treating team discusses whether disease-directed therapy is still justified. Which of the following best reflects how the biopsy findings should influence the treatment decision?
body: A 68-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, reduced appetite, arthralgia, and a purpuric rash over both lower limbs. He has no known history of chronic kidney disease. His current med
full:
A 68-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, reduced appetite, arthralgia, and a purpuric rash over both lower limbs. He has no known history of chronic kidney disease. His current medications include amlodipine for hypertension.
Four weeks ago, his serum creatinine was 1.1 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 71 mL/min/1.73 m2. His blood pressure today is 152/88 mmHg, heart rate is 94 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.1 C. Serum creatinine is now 4.3 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 14 mL/min/1.73 m2. Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing is positive.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 35 to 45 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 2.0 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 20 glomeruli, of which 12 are globally sclerotic. Cellular crescents are present in 4 glomeruli, and segmental fibrinoid necrosis is present in 3 glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
Because of the extensive chronic damage on biopsy, the treating team discusses whether disease-directed therapy is still justified. Which of the following best reflects how the biopsy findings should influence the treatment decision?
A. Proceed with induction treatment because kidney recovery may occur despite advanced histologic damage
B. Provide supportive kidney care alone because extensive glomerulosclerosis predicts irreversible loss of kidney function
C. Defer induction treatment until repeat biopsy shows evidence that the chronic lesions have improved
D. Reserve induction treatment for development of additional extrarenal disease because kidney recovery is unlikely
E. Withhold induction treatment and plan kidney replacement therapy because histologic damage outweighs current disease activity
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: A. Proceed with induction treatment because kidney recovery may occur despite advanced histologic damage
PART C - Explanation
The patient has active ANCA-associated vasculitis with rapidly progressive kidney involvement. Serum creatinine has increased from 1.1 mg/dL to 4.3 mg/dL over four weeks, estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 71 to 14 mL/min/1.73 m2, and the urine sediment demonstrates dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts. The biopsy also demonstrates pauci-immune necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis together with extensive chronic glomerular damage.
More than 50% of the sampled glomeruli are globally sclerotic, a histologic pattern associated with an unfavorable kidney prognosis. Kidney histology is useful for estimating long-term risk of kidney failure. However, KDIGO emphasizes that kidney recovery can still occur despite advanced kidney damage and that induction treatment should not be withheld solely because histologic findings appear unfavorable.

title: Q018 · According to the histopathologic classification of ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis, which class best describes this biopsy?
body: A 52-year-old woman with newly diagnosed myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis presents with fatigue, arthralgia, and declining kidney function. Her past medical history includes hypertension. He
full:
A 52-year-old woman with newly diagnosed myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis presents with fatigue, arthralgia, and declining kidney function. Her past medical history includes hypertension. Her current medications include amlodipine.
Three weeks ago, her serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 68 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure today is 148/86 mmHg, heart rate is 88 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.1 C. Serum creatinine is now 2.9 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 19 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.8 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 20 glomeruli. Three glomeruli are globally sclerotic, 10 are normal, and 7 contain cellular crescents, with focal segmental fibrinoid necrosis also present. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
According to the histopathologic classification of ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis, which class best describes this biopsy?
A. Not classifiable within the histopathologic system
B. Crescentic class
C. Sclerotic class
D. Mixed class
E. Focal class
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. Focal class
PART C - Explanation
The biopsy contains 20 glomeruli. Three of 20 glomeruli, or 15%, are globally sclerotic; 10 of 20, or 50%, are normal; and 7 of 20, or 35%, contain cellular crescents.
The histopathologic classification should be applied in a specific sequence. A biopsy is classified as sclerotic when at least 50% of glomeruli are globally sclerotic. If this criterion is not met, the next step is to determine whether at least 50% of glomeruli are normal. If so, the biopsy is classified as focal. Only if neither of these criteria is satisfied is the proportion of glomeruli with cellular crescents considered; at least 50% cellular crescents defines the crescentic class. Biopsies that meet none of these predominant patterns are classified as mixed.

title: Q019 · When counseling the patient about long-term kidney outcomes, which of the following biopsy profiles would be associated with the most favorable prognosis based on validation studies of the Berden histopathologic classification?
body: A 64-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, reduced appetite, and a purpuric rash over both lower limbs. She has no known history of chronic kidney disease. Her current medications
full:
A 64-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, reduced appetite, and a purpuric rash over both lower limbs. She has no known history of chronic kidney disease. Her current medications include amlodipine for hypertension.
One month ago, her serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 63 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure today is 150/88 mmHg, heart rate is 90 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.1 C. Serum creatinine is now 3.2 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 16 mL/min/1.73 m2. Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing is positive.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.9 g/day. The clinical findings are consistent with newly diagnosed ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis, and a kidney biopsy is planned to provide additional prognostic information.
When counseling the patient about long-term kidney outcomes, which of the following biopsy profiles would be associated with the most favorable prognosis based on validation studies of the Berden histopathologic classification?
A. 20% normal glomeruli, 60% globally sclerotic glomeruli, and 20% glomeruli with cellular crescents
B. 60% normal glomeruli, 20% globally sclerotic glomeruli, and 20% glomeruli with cellular crescents
C. 30% normal glomeruli, 25% globally sclerotic glomeruli, and 45% glomeruli with cellular crescents
D. 45% normal glomeruli, 30% globally sclerotic glomeruli, and 25% glomeruli with cellular crescents
E. 25% normal glomeruli, 40% globally sclerotic glomeruli, and 35% glomeruli with cellular crescents
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: B. 60% normal glomeruli, 20% globally sclerotic glomeruli, and 20% glomeruli with cellular crescents
PART C - Explanation
Kidney histology provides prognostic information in ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis. In validation studies of the Berden histopathologic classification, more than 50% normal glomeruli in the focal class were associated with a favorable kidney outcome, whereas more than 50% globally sclerotic glomeruli were associated with a poor outcome. Outcomes reported for the crescentic and mixed classes have been less consistent.

title: Q020 · Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
body: A 56-year-old man with proteinase 3 ANCA-associated vasculitis was diagnosed three months ago after presenting with fatigue, nasal congestion, purpura, and rapidly declining kidney function. At diagno
full:
A 56-year-old man with proteinase 3 ANCA-associated vasculitis was diagnosed three months ago after presenting with fatigue, nasal congestion, purpura, and rapidly declining kidney function. At diagnosis, his serum creatinine was 3.1 mg/dL, and his estimated glomerular filtration rate was 22 mL/min/1.73 m2. A kidney biopsy was performed, and induction therapy was started.
Six weeks after starting treatment, his extrarenal symptoms had improved, C-reactive protein had decreased from 48 mg/L to 4 mg/L, and kidney function had partially improved. His serum creatinine decreased to 2.5 mg/dL, and his estimated glomerular filtration rate increased to 30 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Over the next six weeks, despite continued treatment, his kidney function worsened. At the current visit, serum creatinine has increased to 3.2 mg/dL, and estimated glomerular filtration rate has decreased to 22 mL/min/1.73 m2. His nasal symptoms, purpura, and constitutional symptoms remain resolved. His blood pressure is 142/84 mmHg, heart rate is 80 beats per minute, and temperature is 36.9 C.
Urinalysis demonstrates 2+ blood and 2+ protein, with 15 to 20 red blood cells per high-power field. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.3 g/day. The treating team is uncertain whether the worsening kidney function reflects ongoing vasculitic activity, residual parenchymal damage, or another kidney process.
The initial kidney biopsy showed focal segmental fibrinoid necrosis and cellular crescents on light microscopy, with areas of interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy. Immunofluorescence showed no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy showed no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
A. Repeat proteinase 3 ANCA testing to determine whether renal vasculitis remains active
B. Repeat kidney biopsy to reassess renal histologic activity and chronic damage
C. Repeat C-reactive protein measurement to determine whether kidney inflammation persists
D. Obtain renal ultrasonography to determine whether the kidney dysfunction reflects active vasculitis
E. Repeat urine protein quantification to determine whether the current kidney injury is reversible
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: B. Repeat kidney biopsy to reassess renal histologic activity and chronic damage
PART C - Explanation
The patient initially improved after treatment. His extrarenal manifestations resolved, C-reactive protein normalized, and kidney function partially recovered, with serum creatinine decreasing from 3.1 mg/dL to 2.5 mg/dL.
However, during the following six weeks, kidney function worsened despite continued treatment. Serum creatinine increased to 3.2 mg/dL, and estimated glomerular filtration rate decreased to 22 mL/min/1.73 m2. Hematuria and proteinuria also persist.
According to KDIGO, assessing kidney remission can be difficult because hematuria and proteinuria may persist after treatment. Stable or falling serum creatinine, control of extrarenal disease, and normalization of inflammatory markers are helpful, but they do not exclude ongoing kidney activity. Other causes of kidney injury unrelated to ANCA-associated vasculitis should also be considered. When treatment response is poor or the cause of persistent kidney dysfunction remains uncertain, repeat kidney biopsy should be considered.

title: Q021 · Which of the following is the most appropriate approach at this time?
body: A 54-year-old man with proteinase 3 ANCA-associated vasculitis was diagnosed nine months ago after presenting with sinus symptoms, purpura, microscopic hematuria, and declining kidney function. At dia
full:
A 54-year-old man with proteinase 3 ANCA-associated vasculitis was diagnosed nine months ago after presenting with sinus symptoms, purpura, microscopic hematuria, and declining kidney function. At diagnosis, serum creatinine was 2.9 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 24 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis demonstrated 3+ blood, 2+ protein, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimated proteinuria of 1.7 g/day. Proteinase 3 ANCA testing was positive, and he received induction therapy.
Three months after starting treatment, his sinus symptoms and purpura had resolved. His Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score was 0. Serum creatinine had decreased to 1.4 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate had increased to 58 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis showed trace blood and trace protein, with 2 to 4 red blood cells per high-power field and no red blood cell casts. Proteinuria was 0.2 g/day. Proteinase 3 ANCA testing had become negative.
At a routine follow-up six months later, he continues to feel well and reports no sinus symptoms, cough, hemoptysis, skin lesions, visual symptoms, or neurologic symptoms. His blood pressure is 136/82 mmHg, heart rate is 76 beats per minute, and temperature is 36.8 C. Serum creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 57 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis again shows trace blood and trace protein, with 2 to 4 red blood cells per high-power field and no red blood cell casts. Proteinuria remains 0.2 g/day. Repeat proteinase 3 ANCA testing is now positive.
Which of the following is the most appropriate approach at this time?
A. Restart induction treatment because conversion to positive ANCA establishes recurrent active vasculitis
B. Increase the frequency of clinical assessment while avoiding treatment escalation based solely on the serologic change
C. Increase immunosuppressive treatment because reappearance of ANCA predicts that clinical relapse is already occurring
D. Continue the usual follow-up schedule because conversion from negative to positive ANCA has no prognostic significance
E. Perform immediate kidney biopsy because reappearance of ANCA alone establishes recurrent glomerular disease
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: B. Increase the frequency of clinical assessment while avoiding treatment escalation based solely on the serologic change
PART C - Explanation
The patient had a favorable clinical response after induction treatment. His extrarenal manifestations resolved, Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score became 0, kidney function improved, urinary abnormalities decreased, and proteinase 3 ANCA became negative. At the current visit, kidney function and urine findings remain stable and no new systemic manifestations have developed, but proteinase 3 ANCA has changed from negative to positive.
According to KDIGO, a change in ANCA status from negative to positive has been associated with a higher incidence of future relapse, and more frequent clinical assessment should be considered. However, ANCA measurements are only modest predictors of relapse and should not independently guide treatment decisions in an individual patient. Reappearance of ANCA therefore warrants increased clinical surveillance rather than a diagnosis of relapse or automatic escalation of immunosuppression.

title: Q022 · Which of the following best describes the significance of the persistent proteinase 3 ANCA positivity in this patient?
body: A 51-year-old man with proteinase 3 ANCA-associated vasculitis was diagnosed six months ago after presenting with fatigue, chronic nasal congestion, purpura, and rapidly declining kidney function. At
full:
A 51-year-old man with proteinase 3 ANCA-associated vasculitis was diagnosed six months ago after presenting with fatigue, chronic nasal congestion, purpura, and rapidly declining kidney function. At diagnosis, his serum creatinine was 3.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 23 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis demonstrated 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimated proteinuria of 1.8 g/day. Proteinase 3 ANCA testing was positive, and he received induction therapy.
Three months after starting treatment, his nasal symptoms, purpura, and constitutional symptoms had resolved. Serum creatinine had decreased to 1.5 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate had increased to 55 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis showed trace blood and trace protein, with 2 to 4 red blood cells per high-power field and no red blood cell casts. Proteinuria had decreased to 0.2 g/day. His Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score was 0. Proteinase 3 ANCA testing, however, remained positive.
At the current visit three months later, he continues to feel well and reports no nasal symptoms, cough, hemoptysis, skin lesions, visual symptoms, or neurologic symptoms. His blood pressure is 134/80 mmHg, heart rate is 74 beats per minute, and temperature is 36.8 C. Serum creatinine is 1.5 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 54 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis remains unchanged, with trace blood and trace protein, 2 to 4 red blood cells per high-power field, and no red blood cell casts. Proteinuria remains 0.2 g/day. Proteinase 3 ANCA testing remains positive.
Which of the following best describes the significance of the persistent proteinase 3 ANCA positivity in this patient?
A. It has no prognostic relevance once clinical remission is achieved and therefore should not be considered in subsequent treatment planning
B. It demonstrates persistent active vasculitis and therefore warrants renewed induction therapy despite the absence of clinical disease activity
C. It establishes kidney relapse and therefore warrants treatment escalation despite stable kidney function and unchanged urinary findings
D. It indicates failure to achieve remission because ANCA negativity is required before a patient can be considered clinically in remission
E. It is a modest predictor of future relapse that may inform overall risk assessment but should not independently determine treatment changes
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. It is a modest predictor of future relapse that may inform overall risk assessment but should not independently determine treatment changes
PART C - Explanation
The patient has responded clinically to induction therapy. His extrarenal manifestations have resolved, his Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score is 0, serum creatinine has improved from 3.0 mg/dL to 1.5 mg/dL, estimated glomerular filtration rate has improved from 23 to 54 mL/min/1.73 m2, and his urinary abnormalities have substantially decreased and remained stable. Despite this clinical improvement, proteinase 3 ANCA remains positive.
According to KDIGO, persistent ANCA positivity after treatment may be predictive of future disease relapse. However, persistence of ANCA is only modestly predictive, and ANCA measurements should not independently guide treatment decisions in individual patients. Persistent positivity therefore contributes to relapse-risk assessment but does not by itself establish active disease, relapse, or a need to escalate immunosuppression.

title: Q023 · When discussing her longer-term disease course, which of the following best describes the significance of the serologic phenotype documented at diagnosis?
body: A 47-year-old woman with ANCA-associated vasculitis was diagnosed eight months ago after presenting with fatigue, chronic nasal congestion, purpura, and rapidly declining kidney function. At diagnosis
full:
A 47-year-old woman with ANCA-associated vasculitis was diagnosed eight months ago after presenting with fatigue, chronic nasal congestion, purpura, and rapidly declining kidney function. At diagnosis, her serum creatinine was 2.8 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 21 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis demonstrated 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimated proteinuria of 1.6 g/day. Proteinase 3 ANCA testing was positive. She received induction therapy.
Three months after starting treatment, her nasal symptoms, purpura, and constitutional symptoms had resolved. Serum creatinine decreased to 1.3 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate increased to 51 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis showed trace blood and trace protein, with 2 to 4 red blood cells per high-power field and no red blood cell casts. Proteinuria decreased to 0.2 g/day. Her Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score was 0.
At her current follow-up five months later, she remains clinically well. Her blood pressure is 132/80 mmHg, heart rate is 72 beats per minute, and temperature is 36.8 C. Serum creatinine remains 1.3 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 52 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urine findings are unchanged, and she has no new extrarenal manifestations.
When discussing her longer-term disease course, which of the following best describes the significance of the serologic phenotype documented at diagnosis?
A. Proteinase 3 ANCA positivity increases relapse tendency only when active kidney dysfunction persists after induction therapy
B. Proteinase 3 ANCA-positive disease is associated with fewer relapses than myeloperoxidase ANCA-positive disease
C. Proteinase 3 ANCA-positive and myeloperoxidase ANCA-positive disease have similar tendencies to relapse after remission
D. Proteinase 3 ANCA-positive disease is associated with more relapses than myeloperoxidase ANCA-positive disease
E. Proteinase 3 ANCA positivity has no relevance to future relapse once clinical remission has been achieved
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: D. Proteinase 3 ANCA-positive disease is associated with more relapses than myeloperoxidase ANCA-positive disease
PART C - Explanation
The patient has achieved a favorable clinical response after induction therapy. Her systemic manifestations have resolved, Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score is 0, kidney function has substantially improved and remained stable, and the urinary abnormalities have decreased. The question therefore concerns longer-term relapse propensity rather than evidence of current disease activity.
According to KDIGO, both proteinase 3 ANCA-associated and myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis can relapse, but patients who are proteinase 3 ANCA positive experience more relapses than patients who are myeloperoxidase ANCA positive. This association can inform longitudinal counseling and relapse-risk assessment, but it does not mean that an individual patient with proteinase 3 ANCA-positive disease will necessarily relapse.

title: Q024 · Which of the following is the most appropriate approach to the current findings?
body: A 49-year-old man with proteinase 3 ANCA-associated vasculitis was diagnosed eight months ago after presenting with fatigue, chronic nasal congestion, purpura, and rapidly declining kidney function. A
full:
A 49-year-old man with proteinase 3 ANCA-associated vasculitis was diagnosed eight months ago after presenting with fatigue, chronic nasal congestion, purpura, and rapidly declining kidney function. At diagnosis, his serum creatinine was 3.1 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 22 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis demonstrated 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimated proteinuria of 1.9 g/day. Proteinase 3 ANCA testing was positive, and he received induction therapy.
Three months after starting treatment, his systemic manifestations had resolved. Serum creatinine had decreased to 1.4 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate had increased to 58 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis showed trace blood and trace protein, with 2 to 4 red blood cells per high-power field and no red blood cell casts. Proteinuria had decreased to 0.2 g/day. His Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score was 0.
At follow-up five months later, he remains clinically well. His blood pressure is 134/80 mmHg, heart rate is 74 beats per minute, and temperature is 36.8 C. Serum creatinine remains 1.4 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 57 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis remains unchanged, with trace blood and trace protein, 2 to 4 red blood cells per high-power field, and no red blood cell casts. Proteinuria remains 0.2 g/day. Serial proteinase 3 ANCA measurements, however, have increased compared with the previous follow-up.
Which of the following is the most appropriate approach to the current findings?
A. Disregard the ANCA increase entirely because serial ANCA measurements have no value in estimating future relapse risk once remission is achieved
B. Diagnose recurrent active vasculitis and restart induction therapy because rising ANCA levels establish relapse before clinical manifestations appear
C. Increase maintenance immunosuppression immediately because a rising ANCA level is sufficient evidence that current treatment is no longer controlling disease
D. Classify the patient as having kidney relapse because increasing ANCA levels indicate renewed renal activity despite stable kidney function and urine findings
E. Consider the ANCA rise as a modest relapse-risk signal, but do not change treatment solely because of the serologic trend
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. Consider the ANCA rise as a modest relapse-risk signal, but do not change treatment solely because of the serologic trend
PART C - Explanation
The patient remains clinically stable after induction therapy. His systemic manifestations remain absent, kidney function is unchanged, urine findings have not worsened, and there is no objective evidence of renewed kidney or extrarenal disease activity. The only new finding is an increase in proteinase 3 ANCA levels.
According to KDIGO, persistence of ANCA positivity, an increase in ANCA levels, or conversion from negative to positive may be predictive of future relapse and should be considered when making treatment decisions. However, these serologic changes are only modestly predictive, and ANCA measurements should not determine treatment decisions by themselves in individual patients.

title: Q025 · The patient has not previously received immunosuppressive treatment for ANCA-associated vasculitis. Which of the following treatment approaches is most appropriate at this stage?
body: A 56-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, nasal congestion, arthralgia, and a new purpuric rash over both lower limbs. She has no previous history of vasculitis or chronic kidney
full:
A 56-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, nasal congestion, arthralgia, and a new purpuric rash over both lower limbs. She has no previous history of vasculitis or chronic kidney disease. Her current medications include amlodipine for hypertension.
Four weeks ago, her serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 74 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure today is 150/88 mmHg, heart rate is 92 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.2 C. Serum creatinine is now 2.8 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 20 mL/min/1.73 m2. Proteinase 3 ANCA testing is positive.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.8 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 18 glomeruli with segmental fibrinoid necrosis in 5 glomeruli and cellular crescents in 6 glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
The patient has not previously received immunosuppressive treatment for ANCA-associated vasculitis. Which of the following treatment approaches is most appropriate at this stage?
A. Begin glucocorticoids together with either rituximab or cyclophosphamide
B. Begin rituximab alone and reserve glucocorticoids for persistent disease activity
C. Begin cyclophosphamide alone and add glucocorticoids only if kidney function worsens
D. Begin glucocorticoids alone and introduce additional immunosuppression only if remission is not achieved
E. Begin mycophenolate mofetil alone and reserve other immunosuppressive agents for subsequent relapse
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: A. Begin glucocorticoids together with either rituximab or cyclophosphamide
PART C - Explanation
The patient has new-onset active ANCA-associated vasculitis with kidney involvement. Her serum creatinine has increased from 0.9 mg/dL to 2.8 mg/dL over four weeks, estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 74 to 20 mL/min/1.73 m2, the urine sediment demonstrates glomerular hematuria and red blood cell casts, and kidney biopsy shows pauci-immune necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis.
KDIGO recommends glucocorticoids in combination with either rituximab or cyclophosphamide as initial treatment for new-onset ANCA-associated vasculitis. The recommendation supports combination therapy rather than use of rituximab, cyclophosphamide, or glucocorticoids as sole initial therapy.

title: Q026 · The treating team is considering glucocorticoids with either rituximab or cyclophosphamide for remission induction. Which of the following best reflects the evidence relevant to this patient?
body: A 64-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, reduced appetite, arthralgia, and a new purpuric rash over both lower limbs. He has no previous history of vasculitis or chronic kidney dis
full:
A 64-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, reduced appetite, arthralgia, and a new purpuric rash over both lower limbs. He has no previous history of vasculitis or chronic kidney disease. His current medications include amlodipine for hypertension.
One month ago, his serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 81 mL/min/1.73 m2. His blood pressure today is 156/90 mmHg, heart rate is 94 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.2 C. Serum creatinine is now 5.2 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 11 mL/min/1.73 m2. Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing is positive.
