Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 40 to 50 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 2.2 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 20 glomeruli with segmental fibrinoid necrosis in 7 glomeruli and cellular crescents in 9 glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
The treating team is considering glucocorticoids with either rituximab or cyclophosphamide for remission induction. Which of the following best reflects the evidence relevant to this patient?
A. Cyclophosphamide is required for induction when serum creatinine is greater than 4 mg/dL because rituximab is ineffective in this setting
B. Rituximab is contraindicated for induction when serum creatinine is greater than 4 mg/dL because kidney recovery has not been demonstrated
C. Rituximab is preferred over cyclophosphamide when serum creatinine is greater than 4 mg/dL because it produces superior kidney outcomes
D. Rituximab and cyclophosphamide have equally robust induction evidence when serum creatinine is greater than 4 mg/dL
E. Rituximab remains an induction option, but evidence supporting its use is limited when serum creatinine is greater than 4 mg/dL
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. Rituximab remains an induction option, but evidence supporting its use is limited when serum creatinine is greater than 4 mg/dL
PART C - Explanation
The patient has new-onset active ANCA-associated vasculitis with substantial kidney involvement. Serum creatinine has increased from 1.0 mg/dL to 5.2 mg/dL over one month, estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 81 to 11 mL/min/1.73 m2, and the urine sediment demonstrates dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts. Kidney biopsy shows pauci-immune necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis.
KDIGO recommends glucocorticoids in combination with either rituximab or cyclophosphamide for initial treatment of new-onset AAV. However, in patients with serum creatinine greater than 4 mg/dL, the available data supporting rituximab for induction are limited. The comparative trials providing the principal evidence for rituximab versus cyclophosphamide did not provide robust evidence in this degree of kidney dysfunction.

title: Q027 · Which of the following induction strategies is best supported for the current presentation?
body: A 46-year-old man was diagnosed with proteinase 3 ANCA-associated vasculitis 18 months ago after presenting with chronic nasal congestion, purpura, hematuria, and rapidly declining kidney function. At
full:
A 46-year-old man was diagnosed with proteinase 3 ANCA-associated vasculitis 18 months ago after presenting with chronic nasal congestion, purpura, hematuria, and rapidly declining kidney function. At diagnosis, his serum creatinine was 2.7 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 28 mL/min/1.73 m2. Kidney biopsy demonstrated pauci-immune necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis. He received induction therapy and subsequently achieved clinical remission.
During remission, his constitutional and upper respiratory symptoms resolved. Serum creatinine improved to 1.3 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate to 63 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis showed trace blood and trace protein, with 2 to 4 red blood cells per high-power field and no red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimated proteinuria of 0.2 g/day.
Twelve months later, he develops a 2-week history of recurrent nasal congestion, fatigue, and a new purpuric rash over both lower limbs. His blood pressure is 148/86 mmHg, heart rate is 88 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.1 C. Serum creatinine is now 2.5 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 31 mL/min/1.73 m2. Proteinase 3 ANCA testing is positive. Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. Proteinuria is now 1.5 g/day.
Which of the following induction strategies is best supported for the current presentation?
A. Glucocorticoids without an additional immunosuppressive agent
B. Glucocorticoids combined with cyclophosphamide
C. Glucocorticoids combined with mycophenolate mofetil
D. Glucocorticoids combined with methotrexate
E. Glucocorticoids combined with rituximab
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. Glucocorticoids combined with rituximab
PART C - Explanation
The patient previously achieved remission and now has recurrent systemic and kidney manifestations, including nasal symptoms, purpura, a rise in serum creatinine from 1.3 mg/dL to 2.5 mg/dL, recurrent glomerular hematuria with red blood cell casts, and increased proteinuria. This represents relapsing proteinase 3 ANCA-associated vasculitis requiring renewed induction treatment.
For relapsing proteinase 3 ANCA-associated vasculitis, evidence from the RAVE subgroup analysis favors rituximab. Among patients with relapsing PR3-AAV, more patients achieved remission with rituximab, with an odds ratio of 3.57 at 6 months and 4.32 at 12 months. KDIGO also notes that rituximab may be preferred in relapsing patients. The subgroup evidence is of lower certainty because of imprecision and reliance on a single study.

title: Q028 · The treating team is considering rituximab or cyclophosphamide with glucocorticoids for renewed remission induction. Which of the following best reflects the evidence regarding treatment selection in this patient?
body: A 58-year-old woman with myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis was diagnosed 10 months ago after presenting with fatigue, purpura, microscopic hematuria, and declining kidney function. At diagnos
full:
A 58-year-old woman with myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis was diagnosed 10 months ago after presenting with fatigue, purpura, microscopic hematuria, and declining kidney function. At diagnosis, her serum creatinine was 2.6 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 24 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis demonstrated 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimated proteinuria of 1.7 g/day. Kidney biopsy showed pauci-immune necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis.
She received induction therapy and subsequently improved. Her serum creatinine decreased to 1.4 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate increased to 45 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis improved to trace blood and trace protein, with 2 to 4 red blood cells per high-power field and no red blood cell casts. Her Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score became 0.
Several months later, she develops recurrent purpura, fatigue, and dark-colored urine. Her blood pressure is 146/84 mmHg, heart rate is 86 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.0 C. Serum creatinine is now 2.3 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 25 mL/min/1.73 m2. Myeloperoxidase ANCA remains positive. Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 25 to 35 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. Proteinuria is 1.4 g/day.
The treating team is considering rituximab or cyclophosphamide with glucocorticoids for renewed remission induction. Which of the following best reflects the evidence regarding treatment selection in this patient?
A. Cyclophosphamide should be avoided because the RAVE subgroup analysis demonstrated inferior remission outcomes in patients with MPO-ANCA disease
B. Rituximab is preferred because MPO-ANCA positivity predicts a higher remission rate with rituximab than with cyclophosphamide
C. Cyclophosphamide is preferred because MPO-ANCA positivity predicts a higher remission rate with cyclophosphamide than with rituximab
D. Rituximab should be avoided because the RAVE subgroup analysis demonstrated inferior remission outcomes in patients with MPO-ANCA disease
E. Rituximab and cyclophosphamide are both supported induction options, with no demonstrated remission advantage for rituximab in the MPO-ANCA subgroup
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. Rituximab and cyclophosphamide are both supported induction options, with no demonstrated remission advantage for rituximab in the MPO-ANCA subgroup
PART C - Explanation
The patient previously achieved remission and now has recurrent systemic and kidney manifestations, including purpura, worsening kidney function, recurrent glomerular hematuria, red blood cell casts, and increased proteinuria. This represents relapsing ANCA-associated vasculitis requiring renewed induction treatment.
Comparative induction studies evaluated rituximab and cyclophosphamide in ANCA-associated vasculitis. In the RAVE subgroup analysis, a greater remission benefit with rituximab was observed in patients with proteinase 3 ANCA-associated disease, particularly those with relapsing disease. In contrast, no association between treatment drug and remission was observed in patients with myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis. Therefore, the available subgroup evidence does not demonstrate a remission advantage for rituximab over cyclophosphamide in this MPO-ANCA-positive patient.

title: Q029 · The treating team plans induction therapy with glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide. The patient asks how intravenous pulse cyclophosphamide compares with continuous oral cyclophosphamide. Which of the following best describes the evidence relevant to this choice?
body: A 60-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, arthralgia, purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. She has no previous history of vasculitis or chronic kidney disease. H
full:
A 60-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, arthralgia, purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. She has no previous history of vasculitis or chronic kidney disease. Her current medications include amlodipine for hypertension.
Four weeks ago, her serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 72 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure today is 148/86 mmHg, heart rate is 90 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.1 C. Serum creatinine is now 2.7 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 20 mL/min/1.73 m2. Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing is positive.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.7 g/day. Kidney biopsy confirms pauci-immune necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis.
The treating team plans induction therapy with glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide. The patient asks how intravenous pulse cyclophosphamide compares with continuous oral cyclophosphamide. Which of the following best describes the evidence relevant to this choice?
A. Intravenous and oral cyclophosphamide have similar cumulative exposure and remission outcomes, while intravenous treatment causes more leukopenia but fewer later relapses
B. Intravenous cyclophosphamide produces higher remission rates and lower cumulative exposure, while oral treatment causes fewer relapses and similar rates of leukopenia
C. Oral cyclophosphamide produces higher remission rates and fewer relapses, while intravenous treatment lowers cumulative exposure without reducing the risk of leukopenia
D. Intravenous and oral cyclophosphamide have similar outcomes, while intravenous treatment reduces cumulative exposure and leukopenia but may be followed by more relapses
E. Oral and intravenous cyclophosphamide have similar relapse and leukopenia rates, while oral treatment achieves comparable outcomes with substantially lower cumulative exposure
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: D. Intravenous and oral cyclophosphamide have similar outcomes, while intravenous treatment reduces cumulative exposure and leukopenia but may be followed by more relapses
PART C - Explanation
The patient has active ANCA-associated vasculitis with kidney involvement and is being treated with a cyclophosphamide-based induction regimen. The treatment decision in question concerns the route of cyclophosphamide administration rather than whether cyclophosphamide is appropriate.
According to KDIGO, continuous oral and intravenous pulse cyclophosphamide have produced similar overall outcomes. Intravenous pulse administration allows a lower cumulative cyclophosphamide dose than continuous oral treatment. In the CYCLOPS study, this lower exposure was associated with a lower rate of leukopenia. However, during longer-term follow-up, more patients treated with intravenous cyclophosphamide tended to experience relapse.

title: Q030 · Cyclophosphamide-based induction is being considered, but the patient asks whether another immunosuppressive approach could reasonably be used for her current presentation. Which of the following is the best-supported alternative?
body: A 44-year-old woman presents with a 4-week history of fatigue, arthralgia, and scattered palpable purpura over both lower limbs. She has no hemoptysis, dyspnea, visual symptoms, neurologic deficits, o
full:
A 44-year-old woman presents with a 4-week history of fatigue, arthralgia, and scattered palpable purpura over both lower limbs. She has no hemoptysis, dyspnea, visual symptoms, neurologic deficits, or other features of immediately organ-threatening disease. Her past medical history includes hypertension. Her current medications include amlodipine.
Six weeks ago, her serum creatinine was 1.1 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 64 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure today is 142/84 mmHg, heart rate is 82 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.0 C. Serum creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 49 mL/min/1.73 m2. Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing is positive. The kidney-function change has occurred gradually without a rapidly progressive decline.
Urinalysis demonstrates 2+ blood and 1+ protein, with 15 to 20 red blood cells per high-power field and dysmorphic red blood cells. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 0.8 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows focal segmental necrotizing glomerular lesions involving 3 of 18 glomeruli, with cellular crescents in 2 glomeruli and preservation of most remaining glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
Cyclophosphamide-based induction is being considered, but the patient asks whether another immunosuppressive approach could reasonably be used for her current presentation. Which of the following is the best-supported alternative?
A. Glucocorticoids combined with mycophenolate mofetil
B. Glucocorticoids combined with methotrexate despite kidney involvement
C. Mycophenolate mofetil alone without accompanying glucocorticoid therapy
D. Glucocorticoids alone without an additional immunosuppressive agent
E. Supportive kidney care alone without induction immunosuppression
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: A. Glucocorticoids combined with mycophenolate mofetil
PART C - Explanation
The patient has newly diagnosed myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis with kidney involvement, but her presentation is not life-threatening and her kidney function is not declining rapidly. Serum creatinine has increased only gradually from 1.1 mg/dL to 1.4 mg/dL over six weeks, and she has no pulmonary hemorrhage, neurologic emergency, or other immediately organ-threatening manifestation.
According to KDIGO, in patients with non-life-threatening disease, excluding those with rapidly progressive kidney disease, mycophenolate mofetil may be considered as an alternative to cyclophosphamide in the MPO-ANCA subgroup. Trials comparing mycophenolate mofetil with cyclophosphamide showed similar remission rates overall, although relapse risk was substantially greater with mycophenolate mofetil in patients with PR3-ANCA-associated disease.

title: Q031 · The treating team is considering mycophenolate mofetil instead of cyclophosphamide for remission induction. Which of the following is the most important concern with this strategy in this patient?
body: A 52-year-old man presents with a 5-week history of fatigue, chronic nasal congestion, arthralgia, and intermittent purpura over both lower limbs. He has no hemoptysis, dyspnea, visual symptoms, or fo
full:
A 52-year-old man presents with a 5-week history of fatigue, chronic nasal congestion, arthralgia, and intermittent purpura over both lower limbs. He has no hemoptysis, dyspnea, visual symptoms, or focal neurologic deficits. His past medical history includes hypertension, treated with amlodipine.
Six weeks ago, his serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 83 mL/min/1.73 m2. His blood pressure today is 146/84 mmHg, heart rate is 84 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.0 C. Serum creatinine is now 1.5 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 55 mL/min/1.73 m2. Proteinase 3 ANCA testing is positive.
Urinalysis demonstrates 2+ blood and 1+ protein, with 15 to 20 red blood cells per high-power field and dysmorphic red blood cells. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 0.9 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows focal segmental necrotizing lesions in 3 of 20 glomeruli and cellular crescents in 2 glomeruli, with preservation of most remaining glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
The treating team is considering mycophenolate mofetil instead of cyclophosphamide for remission induction. Which of the following is the most important concern with this strategy in this patient?
A. Mycophenolate mofetil is unlikely to induce remission because proteinase 3 ANCA-associated disease is intrinsically resistant to this treatment
B. Mycophenolate mofetil may achieve remission, but subsequent relapse risk is substantially greater in proteinase 3 ANCA-associated disease
C. Mycophenolate mofetil carries a substantially greater risk of leukopenia than cyclophosphamide in proteinase 3 ANCA-associated disease
D. Mycophenolate mofetil is associated with poorer short-term kidney recovery than cyclophosphamide despite similar relapse rates
E. Mycophenolate mofetil should be avoided because it has not demonstrated remission induction in any form of ANCA-associated vasculitis
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: B. Mycophenolate mofetil may achieve remission, but subsequent relapse risk is substantially greater in proteinase 3 ANCA-associated disease
PART C - Explanation
The patient has newly diagnosed proteinase 3 ANCA-associated vasculitis with kidney involvement that is not immediately life-threatening and is not presenting with rapidly progressive kidney failure. The question therefore focuses on the comparative evidence for mycophenolate mofetil versus cyclophosphamide rather than on whether the patient requires induction treatment.
According to KDIGO, trials comparing mycophenolate mofetil with cyclophosphamide showed similar remission rates in patients with both proteinase 3 ANCA-associated and myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis. However, in the MYCYC trial, patients with proteinase 3 ANCA-associated disease treated with mycophenolate mofetil had a substantially increased risk of subsequent relapse.

title: Q033 · For which patient does the available evidence most closely support consideration of methotrexate with glucocorticoids for remission induction?
body: A vasculitis clinic is evaluating five patients with newly diagnosed active ANCA-associated vasculitis for induction therapy. All have systemic manifestations requiring treatment, but their patterns o
full:
A vasculitis clinic is evaluating five patients with newly diagnosed active ANCA-associated vasculitis for induction therapy. All have systemic manifestations requiring treatment, but their patterns of organ involvement differ.
Patient A is a 42-year-old woman with fatigue, chronic nasal symptoms, arthralgia, and purpura. Her blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg, heart rate is 78 beats per minute, and temperature is 36.9 C. Serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 92 mL/min/1.73 m2, unchanged from 0.8 mg/dL and 91 mL/min/1.73 m2 six weeks earlier. Urinalysis shows no blood or protein, and urine sediment is bland. She has no evidence of irreversible tissue damage.
Patient B is a 45-year-old man with fatigue, purpura, and dark-colored urine. Serum creatinine has increased from 0.9 mg/dL to 1.7 mg/dL, with estimated glomerular filtration rate decreasing from 96 to 51 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis shows 2+ blood and 1+ protein with dysmorphic red blood cells, and proteinuria is 0.8 g/day.
Patient C is a 50-year-old woman with upper respiratory manifestations and arthralgia. Serum creatinine is stable at 0.9 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 80 mL/min/1.73 m2, and urinalysis is bland. She has established irreversible tissue damage attributable to vasculitis.
Patient D is a 61-year-old man with purpura and rapidly worsening kidney function. Serum creatinine has increased from 1.1 mg/dL to 3.4 mg/dL, with estimated glomerular filtration rate decreasing from 72 to 19 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood and 2+ protein with red blood cell casts, and proteinuria is 1.9 g/day.
Patient E is a 55-year-old woman with constitutional symptoms and persistent microscopic hematuria. Serum creatinine is 1.5 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 43 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis shows 2+ blood and 1+ protein with dysmorphic red blood cells, and proteinuria is 0.7 g/day.
For which patient does the available evidence most closely support consideration of methotrexate with glucocorticoids for remission induction?
A. Patient C
B. Patient B
C. Patient A
D. Patient D
E. Patient E
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: C. Patient A
PART C - Explanation
According to KDIGO, methotrexate with glucocorticoids has been used for ANCA-associated vasculitis without kidney disease and in the absence of irreversible tissue damage. Although this regimen can be used for remission induction in that selected setting, it has been associated with a higher relapse rate and greater late accrual of damage compared with cyclophosphamide.
C is correct because Patient A has active ANCA-associated vasculitis without evidence of kidney involvement. Her serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate are stable, urinalysis is normal, the urine sediment is bland, and there is no irreversible tissue damage. She therefore most closely matches the population in which methotrexate with glucocorticoids has been used.

title: Q034 · He begins induction therapy with rituximab and glucocorticoids. The treating team is determining how rapidly the glucocorticoid dose should be reduced. Which of the following approaches is best supported by the available evidence for this patient?

A 57-year-old man presents with a 4-week history of fatigue, arthralgia, nasal congestion, and purpura over both lower limbs. He has no hemoptysis, respiratory distress, visual symptoms, or focal neurologic deficits. His past medical history includes hypertension treated with amlodipine.
Six weeks ago, his serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 82 mL/min/1.73 m2. His blood pressure today is 152/86 mmHg, heart rate is 88 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.1 C. Serum creatinine is now 2.6 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 27 mL/min/1.73 m2. He begins induction therapy with rituximab and glucocorticoids. The treating team is determining how rapidly the glucocorticoid dose should be reduced. Which of the following approaches is best supported by the available evidence for this patient?
A. Maintain the initial glucocorticoid dose for a prolonged period because an estimated glomerular filtration rate below 50 requires greater exposure
B. Use a standard glucocorticoid taper because more rapid reduction results in lower remission rates when kidney function is impaired
C. Use a more rapid glucocorticoid reduction because it can maintain efficacy while improving safety compared with a standard taper
D. Increase glucocorticoid exposure because reduced dosing is supported only in ANCA-associated vasculitis without kidney involvement

title: Q035 · The treating physician plans remission induction with rituximab and is considering starting prednisolone at 0.5 mg/kg/day rather than 1.0 mg/kg/day. Which of the following best describes how the LoVAS trial evidence applies to this patient?

full:
A 67-year-old Japanese woman presents with a 4-week history of fatigue, arthralgia, purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. She has no hemoptysis or dyspnea and does not require supplemental oxygen. Her past medical history includes hypertension treated with amlodipine.
Six weeks ago, her serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 58 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure today is 148/82 mmHg, heart rate is 86 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.0 C. Serum creatinine is now 2.1 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 24 mL/min/1.73 m2. Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing is positive.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 25 to 30 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.4 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows focal segmental necrotizing lesions and cellular crescents. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for immunoglobulins or complement. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
The treating physician plans remission induction with rituximab and is considering starting prednisolone at 0.5 mg/kg/day rather than 1.0 mg/kg/day. Which of the following best describes how the LoVAS trial evidence applies to this patient?
A. She falls outside the studied population because an estimated glomerular filtration rate below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 was excluded from LoVAS
B. She falls outside the studied population because LoVAS excluded all patients with ANCA-associated kidney disease
C. She falls outside the studied population because LoVAS primarily evaluated proteinase 3 ANCA-associated rather than myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated disease
D. She closely resembles the studied population, supporting reduced-dose prednisolone with rituximab as a reasonable induction approach
E. She should receive high-dose prednisolone because reduced-dose treatment resulted in lower remission rates despite fewer infections
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: D. She closely resembles the studied population, supporting reduced-dose prednisolone with rituximab as a reasonable induction approach
PART C - Explanation
The patient has active myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis with kidney involvement and is being considered for rituximab-based remission induction. Her estimated glomerular filtration rate is 24 mL/min/1.73 m2, which is above the LoVAS exclusion threshold of less than 15 mL/min/1.73 m2, and she has no alveolar hemorrhage requiring supplemental oxygen.
LoVAS compared prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day with prednisolone 1.0 mg/kg/day, with both groups receiving rituximab 375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 doses. Reduced-dose glucocorticoid therapy was noninferior for achieving remission, and the infections that occurred were less severe. The study population was Japanese and predominantly had MPO-ANCA vasculitis, so this patient closely resembles the population studied. However, KDIGO notes that the wider applicability of this regimen to other populations remains uncertain.

title: Q036 · The physician discusses glucocorticoids combined with either rituximab or cyclophosphamide for remission induction. Which of the following best incorporates this patient’s treatment goals into selection of the induction regimen?

Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing is positive.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 25 to 35 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.3 g/day.

The physician discusses glucocorticoids combined with either rituximab or cyclophosphamide for remission induction. Which of the following best incorporates this patient’s treatment goals into selection of the induction regimen?
A. Either regimen must be selected without considering fertility because patient preferences apply only during maintenance therapy
B. Cyclophosphamide should be preferred because fertility concerns do not influence selection between these induction options
C. Rituximab is required because cyclophosphamide cannot be used in any patient who may desire future fertility
D. Rituximab may be preferred because preservation of fertility is an important consideration for this patient

Correct Answer: D. Rituximab may be preferred because preservation of fertility is an important consideration for this patient

The patient has newly diagnosed active ANCA-associated vasculitis with kidney involvement. Her serum creatinine has increased from 0.8 mg/dL to 2.0 mg/dL, estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 102 to 32 mL/min/1.73 m2, and the urine sediment demonstrates dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts. Kidney biopsy supports pauci-immune necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis.
KDIGO recommends glucocorticoids in combination with either rituximab or cyclophosphamide for initial treatment of new-onset ANCA-associated vasculitis. When choosing between these supported induction agents, patient values and preferences are relevant. KDIGO specifically notes that rituximab may be preferred in patients for whom fertility is a concern.

Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing is positive.

A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows focal segmental necrotizing lesions and cellular crescents. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for immunoglobulins or complement. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
The treating team is considering a rituximab-based induction strategy but is concerned about how directly the available prospective evidence applies to his degree of kidney dysfunction. Which of the following best reflects the evidence?
A. Rituximab with cyclophosphamide pulses was inferior to cyclophosphamide for remission induction despite producing fewer treatment-related adverse events
B. Rituximab without cyclophosphamide has prospective evidence showing superior remission induction to cyclophosphamide in patients with serum creatinine greater than 4 mg/dL
C. Rituximab without cyclophosphamide has prospective evidence showing equivalent remission induction to cyclophosphamide across all degrees of severe kidney dysfunction
D. Rituximab-based therapy lacks prospective evidence in severe kidney disease because all randomized trials excluded patients with serum creatinine greater than 4 mg/dL
E. Rituximab with 2 cyclophosphamide pulses and glucocorticoids has prospective evidence showing comparable remission induction and adverse events to cyclophosphamide in severe kidney disease
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. Rituximab with 2 cyclophosphamide pulses and glucocorticoids has prospective evidence showing comparable remission induction and adverse events to cyclophosphamide in severe kidney disease
PART C - Explanation
This patient has new-onset ANCA-associated vasculitis with severe kidney involvement. His serum creatinine has risen from 1.1 mg/dL to 5.1 mg/dL and his estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 72 to 12 mL/min/1.73 m2, accompanied by glomerular hematuria, red blood cell casts, proteinuria, and pauci-immune necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis.
Interpretation of rituximab evidence in this setting requires distinguishing the RAVE and RITUXVAS trials. RAVE excluded patients with severe kidney disease defined by serum creatinine greater than 4 mg/dL. Therefore, RAVE does not provide prospective evidence for rituximab-based remission induction in patients with kidney dysfunction as advanced as that of this patient.
RITUXVAS, however, included patients with severe kidney disease. In that study, rituximab combined with 2 cyclophosphamide pulses and glucocorticoids was comparable with cyclophosphamide for remission induction and for the number of adverse events.

title: Q040 · She asks whether trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole can now be discontinued because the rituximab induction course has been completed. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?

She asks whether trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole can now be discontinued because the rituximab induction course has been completed. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?
A. Continue Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis only while microscopic hematuria remains detectable during follow-up
B. Discontinue Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis immediately after the final rituximab infusion
C. Continue Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis only until kidney function has returned to its previous baseline
D. Continue Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis for 6 months following rituximab induction
E. Discontinue Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis once clinical remission has been achieved after rituximab induction

Correct Answer: D. Continue Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis for 6 months following rituximab induction

The patient has completed rituximab-based remission induction and has achieved a substantial clinical and kidney response. The question concerns the appropriate duration of Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis after rituximab rather than the status of her vasculitis.
According to KDIGO, low-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, or an alternative, is advised for Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis for 6 months following rituximab induction. Therefore, completion of the rituximab infusion course or achievement of clinical remission does not by itself indicate that prophylaxis should be stopped immediately.

title: Q041 · As the usual post-rituximab prophylaxis period is completed, which additional consideration is most appropriate because of his medical history?

The patient has completed rituximab induction and has already received 6 months of Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis, which is the duration advised following rituximab induction. However, he also has pre-existing structural lung disease.
According to KDIGO, longer-term Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis may be considered after rituximab in patients receiving repeated rituximab infusions, those with structural lung disease, and those requiring ongoing immunosuppressive or glucocorticoid therapy.

A 52-year-old woman with myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis was first diagnosed 4 years ago after presenting with purpura, hematuria, and declining kidney function. At that time, she received cyclophosphamide-based induction therapy and accumulated a moderate cumulative exposure to cyclophosphamide before achieving remission. She has had no cyclophosphamide treatment since that time.
During remission, her serum creatinine remained approximately 1.2 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 55 mL/min/1.73 m2. She now presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, recurrent purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. Her blood pressure is 146/84 mmHg, heart rate is 86 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.0 C. Serum creatinine is now 2.3 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 26 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.4 g/day. Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing is positive. Her white blood cell count is within the laboratory reference range.
After consideration of the available induction options, the treating team selects cyclophosphamide with glucocorticoids for treatment of the relapse. Both oral and intravenous cyclophosphamide are available and affordable, and the patient would be able to adhere reliably to an oral regimen. Which route of cyclophosphamide administration is favored based on her treatment history?
A. Oral cyclophosphamide because previous cyclophosphamide exposure favors continuous oral administration
B. Intravenous cyclophosphamide because she already has a moderate cumulative exposure to cyclophosphamide
C. Intravenous cyclophosphamide only if her white blood cell count subsequently falls below the reference range
D. Oral cyclophosphamide because prior cyclophosphamide treatment does not influence selection of administration route
E. Either route should be chosen without considering prior cumulative cyclophosphamide exposure
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: B. Intravenous cyclophosphamide because she already has a moderate cumulative exposure to cyclophosphamide
PART C - Explanation
This patient has recurrent ANCA-associated vasculitis with renewed kidney activity, demonstrated by worsening kidney function, recurrent glomerular hematuria, red blood cell casts, and increased proteinuria. Cyclophosphamide has already been selected for remission induction, so the clinical decision concerns the route of administration rather than the choice of induction agent.
According to KDIGO intravenous cyclophosphamide is favored when a patient already has a moderate cumulative dose of cyclophosphamide. Intravenous administration reduces total cyclophosphamide exposure compared with continuous oral treatment, making prior cumulative exposure an important consideration when selecting the route.

title: Q050 · Which of the following is the most appropriate consideration regarding his ongoing immunosuppressive therapy?
body: A 68-year-old man was diagnosed with myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis 3 months ago after presenting with fatigue, purpura, dark-colored urine, and rapidly progressive kidney failure. He had
full:
A 68-year-old man was diagnosed with myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis 3 months ago after presenting with fatigue, purpura, dark-colored urine, and rapidly progressive kidney failure. He had no pulmonary, upper respiratory, neurologic, ocular, or other extrarenal manifestations. Before this illness, his serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 79 mL/min/1.73 m2.
At presentation, his blood pressure was 158/88 mmHg, heart rate was 92 beats per minute, and temperature was 37.0 C. Serum creatinine was 8.1 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 6 mL/min/1.73 m2, and he required initiation of hemodialysis. Urinalysis demonstrated 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 40 to 50 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimated proteinuria of 2.2 g/day.
A kidney biopsy was performed. Light microscopy showed extensive necrotizing and crescentic glomerular injury. Immunofluorescence showed no significant glomerular staining for immunoglobulins or complement. Electron microscopy showed no significant electron-dense immune deposits. He received induction immunosuppressive therapy.
At his 3-month follow-up, his constitutional symptoms and purpura have completely resolved, and he has developed no extrarenal manifestations. His blood pressure is 136/78 mmHg, heart rate is 72 beats per minute, and temperature is 36.8 C. He remains dialysis-dependent with no meaningful recovery of kidney function.
Which of the following is the most appropriate consideration regarding his ongoing immunosuppressive therapy?
A. Consider discontinuing immunosuppressive therapy because he remains dialysis-dependent after 3 months and has no extrarenal disease manifestations
B. Continue immunosuppressive therapy indefinitely because persistent dialysis dependence indicates ongoing active kidney vasculitis
C. Intensify induction therapy because failure to recover kidney function by 3 months establishes treatment-resistant vasculitis
D. Continue immunosuppressive therapy until dialysis independence is achieved regardless of the absence of extrarenal manifestations
E. Restart a new induction regimen because dialysis dependence alone constitutes evidence of clinical relapse
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: A. Consider discontinuing immunosuppressive therapy because he remains dialysis-dependent after 3 months and has no extrarenal disease manifestations
PART C - Explanation
This patient presented with severe kidney involvement from ANCA-associated vasculitis and required dialysis. After 3 months of immunosuppressive treatment, his systemic manifestations have resolved and he has no extrarenal evidence of active vasculitis, but he remains dialysis-dependent without meaningful kidney recovery.
According to KDIGO Practice Point 9.3.1.5, discontinuation of immunosuppressive therapy should be considered after 3 months in patients who remain on dialysis and have no extrarenal manifestations of disease.

title: Q051 · Which of the following best reflects the recommended oral glucocorticoid plan at this stage?

Her blood pressure is 132/78 mmHg, heart rate is 72 beats per minute, and temperature is 36.8 C. Serum creatinine is 1.3 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 50 mL/min/1.73 m2. Which of the following best reflects the recommended oral glucocorticoid plan at this stage?
A. Increase prednisolone because low-dose therapy at 6 months is insufficient after rituximab induction
B. Continue prednisolone at 5 mg/day beyond 6 months following rituximab induction
C. Complete withdrawal of prednisolone by 6 months following rituximab induction
D. Maintain the current prednisolone dose until all microscopic hematuria has completely resolved
E. Maintain prednisolone until proteinase 3 ANCA becomes negative regardless of clinical remission

Correct Answer: C. Complete withdrawal of prednisolone by 6 months following rituximab induction

This patient had active ANCA-associated vasculitis with kidney involvement and has responded well to rituximab-based remission induction. Her systemic manifestations have resolved, kidney function has substantially improved, red blood cell casts are absent, proteinuria has markedly decreased, and she has reached the 6-month point after induction.
According to KDIGO Practice Point 9.3.1.6, rapid oral glucocorticoid tapering is preferred over slower tapering because the two approaches probably make little or no difference in induction of sustained remission. The recommended 6-month glucocorticoid endpoint differs according to the induction regimen. Following cyclophosphamide induction, oral prednisolone should be reduced to 5 mg/day by 6 months. Following rituximab induction, prednisolone can be withdrawn by 6 months.

B. 0.5 mg/kg/day
C. 1.5 mg/kg/day
D. 2.0 mg/kg/day
E. 2.5 mg/kg/day
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: B. 0.5 mg/kg/day
PART C - Explanation
This patient has active ANCA-associated vasculitis with kidney involvement and has already been selected for oral cyclophosphamide-based remission induction. The question therefore focuses specifically on dose adjustment for age and kidney impairment.
According to KDIGO, the standard oral cyclophosphamide dose is 2 mg/kg/day. The recommended dose is reduced to 1.5 mg/kg/day at age 60 years and to 1.0 mg/kg/day at age 70 years. For patients with GFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2, the dose should be reduced by an additional 0.5 mg/kg/day.
This patient is 72 years old, so the age-adjusted dose is 1.0 mg/kg/day. His estimated glomerular filtration rate is 24 mL/min/1.73 m2, which is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2. Applying the additional kidney-function reduction gives:
1.0 mg/kg/day − 0.5 mg/kg/day = 0.5 mg/kg/day.

Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing is positive.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 35 to 45 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.9 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows focal segmental necrotizing lesions and cellular crescents. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for immunoglobulins or complement. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
The treating team selects a combined rituximab and intravenous cyclophosphamide regimen with glucocorticoids for remission induction. Which of the following dosing schedules most closely matches the alternative combination regimen given in Figure 10?
A. Rituximab 1 g weekly for 4 weeks with intravenous cyclophosphamide 500 mg every 2 weeks for 6 doses
B. Rituximab 1 g at weeks 0 and 4 with intravenous cyclophosphamide 500 mg every 2 weeks for 4 doses
C. Rituximab 1 g at weeks 0 and 2 with intravenous cyclophosphamide 500 mg every 2 weeks for 6 doses
D. Rituximab 1 g at weeks 0 and 2 with intravenous cyclophosphamide 500 mg every 4 weeks for 6 doses
E. Rituximab 1 g at weeks 0 and 2 with intravenous cyclophosphamide 500 mg as 2 doses at weeks 0 and 2
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: C. Rituximab 1 g at weeks 0 and 2 with intravenous cyclophosphamide 500 mg every 2 weeks for 6 doses
PART C - Explanation
This patient has active ANCA-associated vasculitis with substantial kidney involvement and has already been selected for combined rituximab and intravenous cyclophosphamide induction. The question therefore tests recognition of the specific dosing schedule rather than selection of the induction agents themselves.
According to KDIGO, one combined induction regimen consists of rituximab 1 g at weeks 0 and 2 together with intravenous cyclophosphamide 500 mg every 2 weeks for 6 doses.

title: Q057 · Which of the following mycophenolate mofetil adjustments is supported for this patient?
body: A 46-year-old woman presents with a 5-week history of fatigue, arthralgia, and scattered palpable purpura over both lower limbs. She has no hemoptysis, dyspnea, visual symptoms, focal neurologic defic
full:
A 46-year-old woman presents with a 5-week history of fatigue, arthralgia, and scattered palpable purpura over both lower limbs. She has no hemoptysis, dyspnea, visual symptoms, focal neurologic deficits, or other life-threatening manifestations. She has no previous history of ANCA-associated vasculitis or chronic kidney disease.
Six weeks before treatment, her serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 67 mL/min/1.73 m2. At diagnosis, her blood pressure was 140/82 mmHg, heart rate was 80 beats per minute, and temperature was 37.0 C. Serum creatinine was 1.4 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 49 mL/min/1.73 m2. Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing was positive.
Urinalysis demonstrated 2+ blood and 1+ protein, with 15 to 20 red blood cells per high-power field and dysmorphic red blood cells. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimated proteinuria of 0.8 g/day. Her kidney function had declined gradually without a rapidly progressive course.
A kidney biopsy was performed. Light microscopy showed focal segmental necrotizing lesions involving a minority of glomeruli. Immunofluorescence showed no significant glomerular staining for immunoglobulins or complement. Electron microscopy showed no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
Because her disease was non-life-threatening and was not associated with rapidly progressive kidney dysfunction, she began induction therapy with glucocorticoids and mycophenolate mofetil 2000 mg/day in divided doses.
At follow-up, she continues to have fatigue and recurrent purpura. Her serum creatinine is 1.5 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 45 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis continues to show 2+ blood and 1+ protein with dysmorphic red blood cells, and proteinuria remains 0.8 g/day. The treating physician considers the response to mycophenolate mofetil inadequate.
Which of the following mycophenolate mofetil adjustments is supported for this patient?
A. Increase mycophenolate mofetil to 3000 mg/day in divided doses
B. Increase mycophenolate mofetil to 2500 mg/day in divided doses
C. Increase mycophenolate mofetil to 4000 mg/day in divided doses
D. Continue mycophenolate mofetil at 2000 mg/day despite the poor response
E. Reduce mycophenolate mofetil to 1000 mg/day because kidney involvement persists
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: A. Increase mycophenolate mofetil to 3000 mg/day in divided doses
PART C - Explanation
This patient has myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis with a non-life-threatening presentation and without rapidly progressive kidney disease, making mycophenolate mofetil a potential alternative induction agent in the selected clinical setting described by KDIGO. She was appropriately started on mycophenolate mofetil 2000 mg/day in divided doses.
Despite treatment, she continues to have systemic manifestations and persistent kidney findings without meaningful improvement, indicating a poor treatment response.
According to KDIGO, mycophenolate mofetil is given at 2000 mg/day in divided doses for induction therapy and may be increased to 3000 mg/day in divided doses when the treatment response is poor.

title: Q058 · The patient is beginning appropriate induction immunosuppressive therapy. Which of the following additional treatment approaches should be considered based on the severity of his kidney involvement?
body: A 52-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, arthralgia, purpura over both lower limbs, and progressively dark-colored urine. He has no previous history of ANCA-associated vasculitis o
full:
A 52-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, arthralgia, purpura over both lower limbs, and progressively dark-colored urine. He has no previous history of ANCA-associated vasculitis or chronic kidney disease. He reports no hemoptysis or shortness of breath.
Four weeks ago, his serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 86 mL/min/1.73 m2. His blood pressure today is 152/88 mmHg, heart rate is 90 beats per minute, temperature is 37.1 C, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Serum creatinine is now 4.1 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 16 mL/min/1.73 m2. Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing is positive, and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are negative.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 35 to 45 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.9 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows focal segmental necrotizing lesions and cellular crescents. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for immunoglobulins or complement. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
The patient is beginning appropriate induction immunosuppressive therapy. Which of the following additional treatment approaches should be considered based on the severity of his kidney involvement?
A. Add plasma exchange to the induction treatment strategy
B. Add mycophenolate mofetil to the induction treatment strategy
C. Add methotrexate to the induction treatment strategy
D. Extend high-dose glucocorticoid therapy without considering plasma exchange
E. Defer additional treatment until the patient requires dialysis
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: A. Add plasma exchange to the induction treatment strategy
PART C - Explanation
This patient has newly diagnosed active ANCA-associated vasculitis with rapidly worsening kidney involvement. His serum creatinine has increased from 1.0 mg/dL to 4.1 mg/dL over 4 weeks, estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 86 to 16 mL/min/1.73 m2, and the urine sediment demonstrates dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts. Kidney biopsy further supports pauci-immune necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis.
According to KDIGO Practice Point 9.3.1.9, plasma exchange should be considered in patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis who have serum creatinine greater than 3.4 mg/dL, require dialysis, have rapidly increasing serum creatinine, or have diffuse alveolar hemorrhage accompanied by hypoxemia.

title: Q059 · Which of the following additional treatments should be incorporated because of this patient’s serologic overlap?
body: A 47-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of fatigue, arthralgia, reduced urine output, and progressively dark-colored urine. He has no previous history of ANCA-associated vasculitis, anti-glom
full:
A 47-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of fatigue, arthralgia, reduced urine output, and progressively dark-colored urine. He has no previous history of ANCA-associated vasculitis, anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, or chronic kidney disease. He reports no hemoptysis or shortness of breath.
Three weeks ago, his serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 88 mL/min/1.73 m2. His blood pressure today is 156/90 mmHg, heart rate is 92 beats per minute, temperature is 37.0 C, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Serum creatinine is now 5.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 13 mL/min/1.73 m2. Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing is positive, proteinase 3 ANCA testing is negative, and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are also positive.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 40 to 50 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 2.0 g/day.
A kidney biopsy demonstrates extensive necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis. The treating team initiates appropriate immunosuppressive induction therapy for ANCA-associated vasculitis.
Which of the following additional treatments should be incorporated because of this patient’s serologic overlap?
A. Add plasma exchange to the induction treatment strategy
B. Add mycophenolate mofetil to the induction treatment strategy
C. Add methotrexate to the induction treatment strategy
D. Delay additional treatment until anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies become undetectable
E. Continue immunosuppression alone because ANCA positivity eliminates the need for plasma exchange
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: A. Add plasma exchange to the induction treatment strategy
PART C - Explanation
This patient has rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with simultaneous myeloperoxidase ANCA positivity and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody positivity, establishing an overlap syndrome of ANCA-associated vasculitis and anti-glomerular basement membrane disease.
According to KDIGO Practice Point 9.3.1.10, plasma exchange should be added for patients with this double-positive overlap syndrome. Although these patients have features of both disorders, their acute presentation behaves more like anti-glomerular basement membrane disease than typical ANCA-associated vasculitis, supporting initiation of plasma exchange in addition to appropriate immunosuppressive therapy.

title: Q060 · Which of the following best describes the appropriate longer-term treatment consideration for this patient?
body: A 41-year-old woman was diagnosed with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis 7 months ago after presenting with fatigue, arthralgia, reduced urine output, and dark-colored urine. At presentation, her
full:
A 41-year-old woman was diagnosed with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis 7 months ago after presenting with fatigue, arthralgia, reduced urine output, and dark-colored urine. At presentation, her serum creatinine had increased from 0.8 mg/dL to 5.2 mg/dL over 4 weeks, with estimated glomerular filtration rate decreasing from 94 to 11 mL/min/1.73 m2. Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing was positive, proteinase 3 ANCA testing was negative, and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies were also positive.
Urinalysis demonstrated 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 40 to 50 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimated proteinuria of 2.1 g/day. Kidney biopsy demonstrated extensive necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis.
Because of the ANCA and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody overlap, she received plasma exchange together with appropriate induction immunosuppressive therapy.
At her current follow-up, she has no constitutional or extrarenal manifestations. Her blood pressure is 132/78 mmHg, heart rate is 70 beats per minute, and temperature is 36.8 C. Serum creatinine has improved to 1.5 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 44 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis shows trace blood and trace protein, with 2 to 4 red blood cells per high-power field and no red blood cell casts. Proteinuria is 0.2 g/day. Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are now undetectable.
Which of the following best describes the appropriate longer-term treatment consideration for this patient?
A. Continue plasma exchange as long-term maintenance therapy despite achievement of clinical disease control
B. Stop immunosuppressive therapy because undetectable anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies eliminate future relapse risk
C. Withhold maintenance therapy unless anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies subsequently become detectable again
D. Withhold maintenance therapy unless serum creatinine rises and active glomerular urine findings subsequently recur
E. Continue with maintenance therapy because double-positive disease has a tendency to relapse
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. Continue with maintenance therapy because double-positive disease has a tendency to relapse
PART C - Explanation
This patient has overlap disease characterized by simultaneous ANCA positivity and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody positivity. During the acute presentation, double-positive patients behave more like patients with anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, which supports the use of plasma exchange together with appropriate immunosuppressive therapy.
The important longer-term distinction is that double-positive disease does not behave exactly like pure anti-glomerular basement membrane disease. According to KDIGO Practice Point 9.3.1.10, patients who are positive for both ANCA and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies have a tendency to relapse and therefore should receive maintenance therapy.

title: Q061 · Which of the following treatment pathways best reflects the management principles for this patient from the acute presentation through disease control?
body: A 45-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, arthralgia, reduced urine output, purpura over both lower limbs, and progressively dark-colored urine. He has no previous history of ANCA-a
full:
A 45-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, arthralgia, reduced urine output, purpura over both lower limbs, and progressively dark-colored urine. He has no previous history of ANCA-associated vasculitis, anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, or chronic kidney disease.
Four weeks ago, his serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 91 mL/min/1.73 m2. His blood pressure today is 158/90 mmHg, heart rate is 94 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.1 C. Serum creatinine is now 5.4 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 11 mL/min/1.73 m2. Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing is positive, proteinase 3 ANCA testing is negative, and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are positive.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 40 to 50 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 2.2 g/day.
A kidney biopsy demonstrates extensive necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis. Appropriate induction immunosuppressive therapy is initiated. Six months later, his constitutional and skin manifestations have resolved. Serum creatinine has improved to 1.5 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 52 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis now shows trace blood and trace protein, with 2 to 4 red blood cells per high-power field and no red blood cell casts. Proteinuria is 0.2 g/day, and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are no longer detectable.
Which of the following treatment pathways best reflects the management principles for this patient from the acute presentation through disease control?
A. Add plasma exchange during acute treatment, then provide maintenance therapy after disease control because relapse can occur
B. Use induction immunosuppression without plasma exchange, then provide maintenance therapy only while anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies remain detectable
C. Add plasma exchange during acute treatment, then stop immunosuppressive therapy after disease control because future relapse is unlikely
D. Use plasma exchange without induction immunosuppression, then begin maintenance therapy only if kidney manifestations subsequently recur
E. Add plasma exchange during acute treatment, then continue plasma exchange as maintenance therapy after anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies disappear
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: A. Add plasma exchange during acute treatment, then provide maintenance therapy after disease control because relapse can occur
PART C - Explanation
This patient has double-positive disease, with both myeloperoxidase ANCA and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies detected during a presentation of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. This overlap syndrome has important implications for both the acute and longer-term phases of treatment.
According to KDIGO Practice Point 9.3.1.10, plasma exchange should be added in patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody overlap. During the acute presentation, double-positive patients behave more like those with anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, supporting initiation of plasma exchange together with appropriate induction immunosuppression.
However, the longer-term disease behavior differs from pure anti-glomerular basement membrane disease. Double-positive patients have a tendency to relapse and therefore should receive maintenance therapy after disease control has been achieved.

title: Q062 · Appropriate induction immunosuppressive therapy is initiated, and because of the severity of his kidney involvement, the treating team has already decided to add plasma exchange. Which of the following plasma-exchange regimens most closely follows the recommended approach for severe kidney ANCA-associated vasculitis?
body: A 56-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, arthralgia, purpura over both lower limbs, reduced urine output, and progressively dark-colored urine. He has no previous history of ANCA-a
full:
A 56-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, arthralgia, purpura over both lower limbs, reduced urine output, and progressively dark-colored urine. He has no previous history of ANCA-associated vasculitis or chronic kidney disease and reports no hemoptysis or shortness of breath.
Four weeks ago, his serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 84 mL/min/1.73 m2. His blood pressure today is 154/88 mmHg, heart rate is 90 beats per minute, temperature is 37.1 C, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Serum creatinine is now 4.6 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 14 mL/min/1.73 m2. Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing is positive, proteinase 3 ANCA testing is negative, and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are negative.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 35 to 45 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 2.0 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows focal segmental necrotizing lesions and cellular crescents. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for immunoglobulins or complement. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
Appropriate induction immunosuppressive therapy is initiated, and because of the severity of his kidney involvement, the treating team has already decided to add plasma exchange. Which of the following plasma-exchange regimens most closely follows the recommended approach for severe kidney ANCA-associated vasculitis?
A. Seven plasma-exchange treatments over a maximum of 14 days using 60 mL/kg volume replacement exclusively with fresh frozen plasma
B. Five plasma-exchange treatments over a maximum of 7 days using 60 mL/kg volume replacement with albumin substitution
C. Seven plasma-exchange treatments over a maximum of 21 days using 30 mL/kg volume replacement with albumin substitution
D. Ten plasma-exchange treatments over a maximum of 14 days using 30 mL/kg volume replacement with albumin substitution
E. Seven plasma-exchange treatments over a maximum of 14 days using 60 mL/kg volume replacement with albumin substitution
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. Seven plasma-exchange treatments over a maximum of 14 days using 60 mL/kg volume replacement with albumin substitution
PART C - Explanation
This patient has active ANCA-associated vasculitis with severe and rapidly progressive kidney involvement. His serum creatinine has increased from 1.0 mg/dL to 4.6 mg/dL over 4 weeks, estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 84 to 14 mL/min/1.73 m2, and the urine sediment demonstrates dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts. Plasma exchange has already been selected, so the question specifically tests the recommended treatment schedule rather than the indication for plasma exchange.
According to KDIGO, the plasma-exchange regimen for severe kidney ANCA-associated vasculitis consists of 7 treatments over a maximum of 14 days, using a replacement volume of 60 mL/kg with albumin substitution.

title: Q063 · Which of the following plasma-exchange approaches most closely follows the recommended regimen for this presentation?
body: A 49-year-old woman presents with a 10-day history of fatigue, arthralgia, cough, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. Over the past 3 days, she has developed recurrent hemoptysis and dark
full:
A 49-year-old woman presents with a 10-day history of fatigue, arthralgia, cough, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. Over the past 3 days, she has developed recurrent hemoptysis and dark-colored urine. She has no previous history of ANCA-associated vasculitis or chronic kidney disease.
Three weeks ago, her serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 80 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure today is 148/86 mmHg, heart rate is 104 beats per minute, temperature is 37.2 C, and oxygen saturation is 86% on room air. Serum creatinine is now 3.1 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 18 mL/min/1.73 m2. Proteinase 3 ANCA testing is positive, myeloperoxidase ANCA testing is negative, and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are negative.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.6 g/day.
Chest imaging demonstrates bilateral pulmonary infiltrates compatible with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. Appropriate induction immunosuppressive therapy is initiated. Because of diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage with hypoxemia, the treating team also decides to perform plasma exchange.
Which of the following plasma-exchange approaches most closely follows the recommended regimen for this presentation?
A. Perform plasma exchange daily for exactly 14 days regardless of bleeding status, using albumin for replacement
B. Perform 7 plasma-exchange treatments over 14 days, using albumin exclusively for replacement
C. Perform plasma exchange every 3 days until oxygen saturation normalizes, using albumin for replacement
D. Perform plasma exchange daily until the bleeding stops, using fresh frozen plasma for replacement
E. Perform a single plasma-exchange treatment followed by fresh frozen plasma only if hemoptysis recurs
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: D. Perform plasma exchange daily until the bleeding stops, using fresh frozen plasma for replacement
PART C - Explanation
This patient has active ANCA-associated vasculitis with kidney involvement and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage accompanied by hypoxemia. Her oxygen saturation is 86% on room air, and chest imaging demonstrates bilateral pulmonary infiltrates compatible with alveolar hemorrhage. Plasma exchange has already been selected, so the question specifically tests the appropriate schedule and replacement fluid for this pulmonary presentation.
According to KDIGO, when plasma exchange is used for diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage, it should be performed daily until the bleeding stops. Fresh frozen plasma is used for replacement in this setting rather than albumin alone.

title: Q064 · Which of the following is the most appropriate maintenance strategy after successful induction of remission?
body: A 58-year-old woman was diagnosed with myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis 5 months ago after presenting with fatigue, nasal congestion, purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. A
full:
A 58-year-old woman was diagnosed with myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis 5 months ago after presenting with fatigue, nasal congestion, purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. At diagnosis, her serum creatinine had increased from 0.9 mg/dL to 2.9 mg/dL over 5 weeks, with estimated glomerular filtration rate decreasing from 72 to 18 mL/min/1.73 m2. Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing was positive and proteinase 3 ANCA testing was negative.
Urinalysis demonstrated 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimated proteinuria of 1.7 g/day.
A kidney biopsy was performed. Light microscopy showed focal segmental necrotizing lesions and cellular crescents. Immunofluorescence showed no significant glomerular staining for immunoglobulins or complement. Electron microscopy showed no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
She received induction therapy with cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids. At her current visit, her fatigue, nasal symptoms, and purpura have resolved. Her blood pressure is 134/80 mmHg, heart rate is 72 beats per minute, and temperature is 36.8 C. Serum creatinine has improved to 1.3 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 48 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis shows trace blood and trace protein, with 2 to 4 red blood cells per high-power field and no red blood cell casts. Proteinuria has decreased to 0.2 g/day. Her Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score is 0.
Which of the following is the most appropriate maintenance strategy after successful induction of remission?
A. Discontinue all immunosuppressive therapy because a Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score of 0 eliminates the need for maintenance
B. Maintenance therapy with mycophenolate mofetil because it is more effective than azathioprine at preventing relapse
C. Continue cyclophosphamide as long-term maintenance because it prevents relapse more effectively than azathioprine
D. Maintenance therapy with either rituximab or azathioprine together with low-dose glucocorticoids
E. Use trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole alone as maintenance therapy because it provides equivalent relapse prevention
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: D. Maintenance therapy with either rituximab or azathioprine together with low-dose glucocorticoids
PART C - Explanation
This patient has achieved remission after induction therapy. Her extrarenal manifestations have resolved, kidney function has substantially improved, urinary abnormalities have markedly decreased, and her Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score is 0. The clinical question therefore concerns how remission should be maintained rather than whether further induction therapy is required.
According to KDIGO Recommendation 9.3.2.1, maintenance therapy after induction of remission should consist of either rituximab or azathioprine combined with low-dose glucocorticoids. The purpose of maintenance therapy is to reduce the risk of subsequent disease relapse.

title: Q065 · The treating team is now selecting a maintenance agent. Which of the following is favored for this patient?
body: A 56-year-old man was diagnosed with myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis 3 years ago after presenting with fatigue, purpura, dark-colored urine, and rapidly declining kidney function. At diagno
full:
A 56-year-old man was diagnosed with myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis 3 years ago after presenting with fatigue, purpura, dark-colored urine, and rapidly declining kidney function. At diagnosis, his serum creatinine had increased from 1.0 mg/dL to 2.8 mg/dL over 5 weeks, with estimated glomerular filtration rate decreasing from 77 to 22 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis demonstrated 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimated proteinuria of 1.8 g/day. Kidney biopsy demonstrated pauci-immune necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis. He received induction therapy and subsequently achieved remission.
Eighteen months later, after a period of stable kidney function, he developed recurrent purpura and dark-colored urine. Serum creatinine increased from 1.3 mg/dL to 2.5 mg/dL, with estimated glomerular filtration rate decreasing from 58 to 29 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis again demonstrated 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. Proteinuria increased from 0.2 g/day to 1.5 g/day. The findings were consistent with a clinical relapse.
He received induction therapy with rituximab. At his current assessment, his purpura has resolved, serum creatinine has improved to 1.4 mg/dL, and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 54 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis shows trace blood and trace protein, with 2 to 4 red blood cells per high-power field and no red blood cell casts. Proteinuria is 0.2 g/day. His Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score is 0.
The treating team is now selecting a maintenance agent. Which of the following is favored for this patient?
A. Mycophenolate mofetil maintenance because it prevents relapse more effectively than either rituximab or azathioprine
B. Azathioprine maintenance because it reduced both major and minor relapses compared with rituximab after rituximab induction
C. Rituximab maintenance because it reduced both major and minor relapses compared with azathioprine in relapsing AAV after rituximab induction
D. Cyclophosphamide maintenance because continued exposure provides superior long-term relapse prevention after rituximab induction
E. No maintenance therapy because successful rituximab reinduction eliminates the subsequent risk of disease relapse
PART B - Correct Answer
Correct Answer: C. Rituximab maintenance because it reduced both major and minor relapses compared with azathioprine in relapsing AAV after rituximab induction
PART C - Explanation
This patient has a documented history of relapsing ANCA-associated vasculitis and has now achieved another remission following rituximab induction. His systemic manifestations have resolved, kidney function has improved, active glomerular urinary findings have subsided, and his Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score is 0. The current decision therefore concerns prevention of another relapse.
According to KDIGO, rituximab is preferred for maintenance therapy particularly in patients with known relapsing disease and after rituximab induction. In RITAZAREM, patients with relapsing ANCA-associated vasculitis who achieved remission following rituximab induction were treated with rituximab or azathioprine for maintenance. Rituximab maintenance decreased both major and minor disease relapses compared with azathioprine. No difference in infection rate was found between the two maintenance strategies.

title: Q066 · The treating team is considering either continuing cyclophosphamide for a prolonged course or transitioning to azathioprine-based maintenance therapy. Which of the following best reflects the evidence relevant to this decision?

B. Continue cyclophosphamide for 12 months because it provides superior relapse prevention with less leukopenia than azathioprine

This patient has achieved remission after approximately 3 months of cyclophosphamide-based induction therapy. Her systemic manifestations have resolved, kidney function has substantially improved, active glomerular urinary findings have subsided, proteinuria has decreased, and her Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score is 0. The clinical issue is therefore how best to maintain remission while limiting unnecessary prolonged cyclophosphamide exposure.
According to KDIGO, azathioprine given after at least approximately 3 months of cyclophosphamide induction was equally effective for relapse prevention compared with extending cyclophosphamide treatment for 12 months. Importantly, transitioning to azathioprine was associated with less leukopenia.

title: Q067 · The treating team is choosing between azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil for maintenance therapy, and the treating physician is wondering which would be the better option. Which of the following best reflects the available evidence?
