Her blood pressure is 148/86 mmHg, heart rate is 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, temperature is 37.1 C, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with more than 50 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. Estimated proteinuria is 1.3 g/day.

The nephrologist elects to use the reduced-dose glucocorticoid plus rituximab regimen studied in LoVAS.
Which of the following most accurately describes the treatment regimen for this patient?
A. Begin prednisolone 30 mg/day, taper to 10 mg/day by month 5 without discontinuation, and administer rituximab 375 mg/m2 intravenously once weekly for 2 doses
B. Begin prednisolone 60 mg/day, taper to 10 mg/day by month 5, and administer rituximab 375 mg/m2 intravenously once weekly for 4 doses
C. Begin prednisolone 30 mg/day, taper with planned discontinuation by month 5, and administer rituximab 375 mg/m2 intravenously once weekly for 4 doses
D. Begin prednisolone 30 mg/day, continue the same dose through month 5, and administer rituximab 1 g intravenously on days 1 and 15
E. Begin prednisolone 60 mg/day, discontinue prednisolone by month 5, and administer rituximab 375 mg/m2 intravenously once monthly for 4 doses
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: C. Begin prednisolone 30 mg/day, taper with planned discontinuation by month 5, and administer rituximab 375 mg/m2 intravenously once weekly for 4 doses
PART C — Explanation
C is correct. In the reduced-dose LoVAS regimen, prednisolone was started at 0.5 mg/kg/day. For this 60-kg patient:
0.5 mg/kg/day × 60 kg = 30 mg/day.
Prednisolone was then tapered with planned discontinuation at 5 months in the reduced-dose group. 
Both treatment groups also received rituximab 375 mg/m2 by intravenous infusion once weekly for 4 doses. The first rituximab dose was administered between day 1 and day 7. 
Thus, the reduced-dose LoVAS strategy for this patient consists of initial prednisolone 30 mg/day with tapering toward discontinuation by month 5, together with four weekly rituximab infusions at 375 mg/m2.
The protocol did allow initiation of the final prednisolone-discontinuation step to be postponed if BVAS had not reached 0 or if CRP and ANCA values had not normalized.

title: Q169 · According to the LoVAS definition, how should her disease status at month 6 be classified?

At diagnosis, serum creatinine is 1.9 mg/dL compared with 0.9 mg/dL 6 weeks earlier. Estimated glomerular filtration rate is 30 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with more than 50 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. Estimated proteinuria is 1.4 g/day.

Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
She receives induction therapy according to the LoVAS protocol. At month 6, the palpable purpura and urinary abnormalities have resolved, and serum creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL. Mild nasal crusting remains unchanged and is scored as the only persistent BVAS version 3 item, giving a total BVAS of 1. She is taking prednisolone 5 mg/day.
According to the LoVAS definition, how should her disease status at month 6 be classified?
A. She does not meet the definition of remission because any residual clinical manifestation prevents remission despite a low BVAS
B. She does not meet the definition of remission because BVAS must be exactly 0 regardless of whether the remaining item is persistent
C. She does not meet the definition of remission because prednisolone must be completely discontinued before remission can be assigned
D. She meets the definition of remission only if the persistent BVAS item resolves before the month 6 assessment
E. She meets the definition of remission because BVAS is 1 with only a persistent item and prednisolone is 10 mg/day or lower
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. She meets the definition of remission because BVAS is 1 with only a persistent item and prednisolone is 10 mg/day or lower
PART C — Explanation
E is correct. In LoVAS, remission at 6 months was defined as a Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score version 3 of 0, or a score of 1 or less when all remaining items were persistent, together with an oral prednisolone dose of 10 mg/day or lower. 
At month 6, this patient has a BVAS of 1, and the only remaining manifestation—mild nasal crusting—is explicitly described as persistent rather than newly active. She is also receiving prednisolone 5 mg/day, which is below the permitted maximum of 10 mg/day. She therefore satisfies the LoVAS definition of remission.

He receives induction therapy according to the LoVAS protocol. At month 2, the palpable purpura and nasal crusting have resolved, urinary abnormalities have improved, and remission is achieved.
At month 4, palpable purpura newly reappears over both lower limbs and is scored as a new BVAS version 3 item.
According to the LoVAS definition, how should this change in disease status be classified?
A. Persistent disease, because the manifestation occurred within 6 months of starting induction therapy
B. Relapse, because at least 1 BVAS item newly emerged after remission had been achieved
C. Treatment failure, because any BVAS item occurring before month 6 prevents classification as relapse
D. Sustained remission, because only a single BVAS item has appeared after the prior remission
E. Incomplete remission, because relapse requires recurrence of multiple BVAS items after remission

Correct Answer: B. Relapse, because at least 1 BVAS item newly emerged after remission had been achieved
PART C — Explanation
B is correct. In LoVAS, relapse was defined as the new emergence or recurrence of 1 or more Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score version 3 items after remission had been achieved. 
This patient achieved remission at month 2. At month 4, palpable purpura newly reappears and is scored as a BVAS item. Because a BVAS manifestation has emerged after prior remission, this meets the LoVAS definition of relapse.

She is beginning rituximab-based induction therapy. The nephrologist reviews the LoVAS trial when deciding whether to use the reduced-dose or high-dose prednisolone regimen.
Which of the following treatment approaches is best supported by the LoVAS results?
A. Use reduced-dose prednisolone only when rituximab cannot be administered because the reduced-dose regimen was studied without rituximab
B. Prefer high-dose prednisolone with rituximab because reduced-dose prednisolone produced substantially fewer remissions at 6 months
C. Use reduced-dose prednisolone with rituximab because it was noninferior to high-dose prednisolone for remission at 6 months
D. Prefer high-dose prednisolone because LoVAS demonstrated superiority of high-dose therapy for remission at 6 months
E. Avoid reduced-dose prednisolone because LoVAS failed to establish noninferiority for remission at 6 months
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: C. Use reduced-dose prednisolone with rituximab because it was noninferior to high-dose prednisolone for remission at 6 months
PART C — Explanation
C is correct. LoVAS was a randomized noninferiority trial comparing reduced-dose prednisolone plus rituximab with high-dose prednisolone plus rituximab in patients with newly diagnosed ANCA-associated vasculitis without severe glomerulonephritis or alveolar hemorrhage. LoVAS
At 6 months, remission was achieved in:
Reduced-dose prednisolone plus rituximab:
49 of 69 patients, 71.0%
High-dose prednisolone plus rituximab:
45 of 65 patients, 69.2%
The absolute difference was +1.8 percentage points. The lower bound of the one-sided 97.5% confidence interval was −13.7 percentage points. Because this remained above the prespecified noninferiority margin of −20 percentage points, the reduced-dose regimen satisfied the trial's criterion for noninferiority. The P value for noninferiority was .003. 
Thus, in a patient who resembles the LoVAS population, reduced-dose prednisolone combined with rituximab can be used as an induction strategy without a demonstrated loss of 6-month remission efficacy beyond the prespecified noninferiority margin.

Which of the following treatment approaches is best supported by the LoVAS results?
A. Use reduced-dose prednisolone only if rituximab is withheld because the safety advantage was demonstrated without concomitant B-cell depletion
B. Prefer high-dose prednisolone with rituximab because it produced higher 6-month remission rates and fewer serious infectious complications
C. Use reduced-dose prednisolone with rituximab because it was noninferior for 6-month remission and was associated with fewer serious adverse events and serious infections
D. Prefer high-dose prednisolone because the reduced-dose regimen lowered infection risk but failed to meet the prespecified remission noninferiority criterion
E. Consider both regimens equivalent in safety because LoVAS demonstrated no numerical or statistical differences in serious adverse events or serious infections
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: C. Use reduced-dose prednisolone with rituximab because it was noninferior for 6-month remission and was associated with fewer serious adverse events and serious infections
PART C — Explanation
C is correct. LoVAS demonstrated that reduced-dose prednisolone plus rituximab was noninferior to high-dose prednisolone plus rituximab for the primary endpoint of remission at 6 months. In addition, serious adverse events and serious infections occurred less frequently in the reduced-dose group. LoVAS
Serious adverse events occurred as follows:
Reduced-dose group:
21 events in 13 patients, 18.8%
High-dose group:
41 events in 24 patients, 36.9%
The absolute difference was −18.1 percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval of −33.0 to −3.2 and P = .02.
Serious infections occurred as follows:
Reduced-dose group:
7 events in 5 patients, 7.2%
High-dose group:
20 events in 13 patients, 20.0%
The absolute difference was −12.8 percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval of −24.2 to −1.3 and P = .04. 
Thus, for a patient resembling the LoVAS population, the reduced-dose prednisolone regimen preserved the trial's primary noninferiority result for remission while being associated with fewer serious adverse events and serious infections.
However, these safety outcomes were secondary endpoints. Because the trial performed multiple secondary comparisons, the authors specified that secondary endpoint findings should be interpreted as exploratory because of the potential for type I error. Therefore, these findings support an association with fewer serious complications in LoVAS but should not be interpreted as definitive proof that the reduced-dose regimen is universally safer in every patient.

B. Reduced-dose prednisolone significantly increased the risk of early relapse compared with high-dose prednisolone
C. High-dose prednisolone completely prevented early relapse and was therefore superior for relapse prevention
D. Reduced-dose and high-dose prednisolone were demonstrated to be equivalent with respect to early relapse risk
E. Reduced-dose prednisolone did not demonstrate a statistically significant difference in early relapse compared with high-dose prednisolone
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. Reduced-dose prednisolone did not demonstrate a statistically significant difference in early relapse compared with high-dose prednisolone
PART C — Explanation
E is correct. In LoVAS, early relapse within 6 months occurred in 3 patients in the reduced-dose group, representing 4.3%, compared with no patients in the high-dose group. The between-group difference was approximately 4.3 percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval crossing 0 and P = .24. Therefore, the trial did not demonstrate a statistically significant difference in early relapse between the treatment groups. 
Although all 3 observed early relapses occurred in the reduced-dose group, this numerical imbalance does not establish that reduced-dose prednisolone increases relapse risk.

title: Q174 · Which of the following treatment approaches is best supported by CYCAZAREM?
body: A 54-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of fatigue, weight loss, myalgia, palpable purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. His blood pressure is 152/88 mmHg, heart rate is 86 b
full:
A 54-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of fatigue, weight loss, myalgia, palpable purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. His blood pressure is 152/88 mmHg, heart rate is 86 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, temperature is 37.2 C, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. MPO-ANCA testing is positive, and he is diagnosed with newly diagnosed microscopic polyangiitis with generalized ANCA-associated vasculitis.
At diagnosis, serum creatinine is 2.3 mg/dL compared with 1.0 mg/dL 8 weeks earlier. Estimated glomerular filtration rate is 31 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with more than 50 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. Estimated proteinuria is 1.6 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 24 glomeruli, with segmental fibrinoid necrosis involving 7 glomeruli and cellular crescents involving 8 glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
He receives oral cyclophosphamide and prednisolone for induction therapy. At month 3, his constitutional symptoms and palpable purpura have resolved, urinary abnormalities have substantially improved, and he achieves remission.
The nephrologist reviews CYCAZAREM when deciding whether continued cyclophosphamide is required for maintenance of remission.
Which of the following treatment approaches is best supported by CYCAZAREM?
A. Withdraw both cyclophosphamide and prednisolone immediately once remission is achieved
B. Continue cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/day indefinitely while discontinuing prednisolone at remission
C. Withdraw cyclophosphamide and continue prednisolone alone without another maintenance immunosuppressive agent
D. Continue cyclophosphamide 1.5 mg/kg/day throughout the entire 18-month study period without substitution
E. Withdraw cyclophosphamide and substitute azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day while continuing prednisolone
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. Withdraw cyclophosphamide and substitute azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day while continuing prednisolone
PART C — Explanation
E is correct. CYCAZAREM evaluated whether cyclophosphamide exposure could be reduced once remission had been achieved in patients with newly diagnosed generalized ANCA-associated vasculitis.
All patients initially received oral cyclophosphamide and prednisolone for at least 3 months. After remission, patients were randomized either to substitute azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day for cyclophosphamide or to continue cyclophosphamide at 1.5 mg/kg/day. Both groups continued prednisolone. 
During the 18-month study period, relapse occurred in:
Azathioprine group:
11 of 71 patients, 15.5%
Continued cyclophosphamide group:
10 of 73 patients, 13.7%
The difference was not statistically significant, with P = .65. The investigators therefore concluded that withdrawing cyclophosphamide and substituting azathioprine after remission did not increase the observed relapse rate during the study period.

She receives oral cyclophosphamide and prednisolone for induction therapy and achieves remission at month 3. The nephrologist is deciding whether to continue cyclophosphamide or substitute azathioprine for maintenance therapy and reviews CYCAZAREM with particular attention to relapse prevention.
Which of the following best reflects the CYCAZAREM findings?
A. Azathioprine was associated with an unacceptable increase in relapse and therefore should not replace cyclophosphamide after remission
B. Continued cyclophosphamide significantly reduced relapse compared with substitution of azathioprine
C. Substitution of azathioprine significantly reduced relapse compared with continued cyclophosphamide
D. Azathioprine and cyclophosphamide were proven to be equivalent for relapse prevention
E. Substitution of azathioprine after remission did not demonstrate a higher relapse rate than continued cyclophosphamide

Correct Answer: E. Substitution of azathioprine after remission did not demonstrate a higher relapse rate than continued cyclophosphamide

E is correct. Relapse was the primary endpoint in CYCAZAREM. The difference was 1.8 percentage points, with P = .65. 
The investigators therefore concluded that withdrawing cyclophosphamide and substituting azathioprine after remission did not increase the observed relapse rate during the study period.

title: Q176 · According to the CYCAZAREM regimen, which of the following is the appropriate maintenance treatment for this patient after remission?

A 58-year-old man weighing 70 kg presents with a 6-week history of fatigue, weight loss, arthralgia, palpable purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. His blood pressure is 148/86 mmHg, heart rate is 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, temperature is 37.1 C, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. PR3-ANCA testing is positive, and he is diagnosed with newly diagnosed granulomatosis with polyangiitis with generalized ANCA-associated vasculitis.
At diagnosis, serum creatinine is 2.0 mg/dL compared with 0.9 mg/dL 7 weeks earlier. Estimated glomerular filtration rate is 37 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with more than 50 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. Estimated proteinuria is 1.4 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 22 glomeruli, with segmental fibrinoid necrosis involving 6 glomeruli and cellular crescents involving 7 glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
He receives oral cyclophosphamide and prednisolone for induction therapy and achieves remission at month 3. The nephrologist elects to withdraw cyclophosphamide and use the azathioprine maintenance strategy studied in CYCAZAREM.
According to the CYCAZAREM regimen, which of the following is the appropriate maintenance treatment for this patient after remission?
A. Azathioprine 105 mg/day with continued prednisolone
B. Azathioprine 140 mg/day with continued prednisolone
C. Azathioprine 70 mg/day with continued prednisolone
D. Cyclophosphamide 140 mg/day with continued prednisolone
E. Cyclophosphamide 105 mg/day with continued prednisolone
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: B. Azathioprine 140 mg/day with continued prednisolone
PART C — Explanation
B is correct. In CYCAZAREM, patients who achieved remission and were assigned to the azathioprine maintenance strategy had cyclophosphamide withdrawn and received azathioprine at 2 mg/kg/day while continuing prednisolone.
For this 70-kg patient:
2 mg/kg/day × 70 kg = 140 mg/day.
Therefore, after remission at month 3, the appropriate initial maintenance regimen is azathioprine 140 mg/day with continued prednisolone.
At 12 months after study entry, the CYCAZAREM protocol reduced azathioprine to 1.5 mg/kg/day, and both treatment groups then received this azathioprine dose together with prednisolone 7.5 mg/day until the end of the 18-month study period. For this 70-kg patient:
1.5 mg/kg/day × 70 kg = 105 mg/day.
Thus, the patient would initially receive azathioprine 140 mg/day after remission, followed by a reduction to 105 mg/day at month 12, with prednisolone continued according to the study protocol.

title: Q177 · Which of the following best describes whether this patient is well represented in CYCAZAREM?
body: A 49-year-old woman presents with a 6-week history of progressive fatigue, reduced appetite, unintentional weight loss, diffuse myalgia, palpable purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine.
full:
A 49-year-old woman presents with a 6-week history of progressive fatigue, reduced appetite, unintentional weight loss, diffuse myalgia, palpable purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. Over the preceding 10 days, she has also noted worsening lower-limb edema and a reduction in urine output. Her blood pressure is 162/94 mmHg, heart rate is 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, temperature is 37.3 C, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. MPO-ANCA testing is positive, and she is diagnosed with newly diagnosed microscopic polyangiitis.
Serum creatinine is 6.2 mg/dL compared with 1.1 mg/dL 7 weeks earlier. Blood urea nitrogen is 74 mg/dL. Estimated glomerular filtration rate is markedly reduced.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with more than 50 red blood cells per high-power field, numerous dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. Estimated proteinuria is 2.1 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 25 glomeruli, with segmental fibrinoid necrosis involving 9 glomeruli and cellular crescents involving 11 glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
The nephrologist reviews CYCAZAREM while considering how directly the trial population and treatment strategy apply to this patient.
Which of the following best describes whether this patient is well represented in CYCAZAREM?
A. She is not well represented because CYCAZAREM excluded patients with serum creatinine greater than 5.7 mg/dL
B. She is well represented because CYCAZAREM included all patients with biopsy-confirmed microscopic polyangiitis regardless of the severity of renal dysfunction
C. She is well represented because the renal exclusion criterion applied only to patients who had already started dialysis
D. She is not well represented because microscopic polyangiitis was not included among the diagnoses studied in CYCAZAREM
E. She is not well represented because CYCAZAREM excluded patients with renal involvement and studied only nonrenal generalized vasculitis
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: A. She is not well represented because CYCAZAREM excluded patients with serum creatinine greater than 5.7 mg/dL
PART C — Explanation
A is correct. CYCAZAREM excluded patients with a serum creatinine concentration greater than 5.7 mg/dL, equivalent to 500 µmol/L. 
This patient otherwise has features that fit the disease spectrum studied in CYCAZAREM: newly diagnosed microscopic polyangiitis with renal involvement and MPO-ANCA positivity. However, her serum creatinine is 6.2 mg/dL, which exceeds the trial’s upper renal-function threshold.
Therefore, she is not well represented in the CYCAZAREM population, and the trial findings cannot be directly generalized to a patient with this degree of renal dysfunction.

MPO-ANCA testing is positive, and he is diagnosed with newly diagnosed microscopic polyangiitis with generalized ANCA-associated vasculitis.
Serum creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL compared with 1.0 mg/dL 7 weeks earlier. Estimated glomerular filtration rate is 29 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with more than 50 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. Estimated proteinuria is 1.7 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 24 glomeruli, with segmental fibrinoid necrosis involving 7 glomeruli and cellular crescents involving 8 glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
The nephrologist elects to begin the oral cyclophosphamide and prednisolone induction regimen used in CYCAZAREM.
According to the CYCAZAREM protocol, what is the appropriate initial daily dose of oral cyclophosphamide for this patient?
A. 70 mg/day
B. 140 mg/day
C. 105 mg/day
D. 90 mg/day
E. 115 mg/day
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. 115 mg/day
PART C — Explanation
E is correct. During remission-induction therapy in CYCAZAREM, oral cyclophosphamide was administered at 2 mg/kg/day. However, the protocol specified that the cyclophosphamide dose should be reduced by 25 mg in patients older than 60 years. 
For this 70-kg patient:
2 mg/kg/day × 70 kg = 140 mg/day
Because he is 65 years old:
140 mg/day − 25 mg = 115 mg/day
Therefore, the appropriate initial oral cyclophosphamide dose according to the CYCAZAREM protocol is 115 mg/day.

Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with more than 50 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. Estimated proteinuria is 1.5 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 24 glomeruli, with segmental fibrinoid necrosis involving 7 glomeruli and cellular crescents involving 8 glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
He receives cyclophosphamide and prednisolone for induction therapy and achieves remission at month 3. At that time, the palpable purpura and constitutional symptoms have resolved, serum creatinine has improved to 1.2 mg/dL, and urinalysis no longer demonstrates red blood cell casts.
At month 9, he again develops dark-colored urine and lower-limb edema. Serum creatinine has increased to 2.7 mg/dL. Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood, more than 50 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and recurrent red blood cell casts. These findings are attributed to recurrent active renal vasculitis.
According to the CYCAZAREM disease definitions, how should this event at month 9 be classified?
A. Continued remission with residual renal damage
B. Minor relapse
C. Persistent disease without relapse
D. Major relapse
E. Primary treatment failure
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: D. Major relapse
PART C — Explanation
D is correct. CYCAZAREM defined major relapse as the recurrence or first appearance of at least 1 of 24 BVAS items indicating threatened function of a vital organ attributable to active vasculitis. The specified vital organs included the kidney, lung, brain, eye, motor nerve, and gut. 
This patient achieved remission at month 3, with improvement in kidney function and disappearance of the active urinary findings. At month 9, he develops recurrent renal vasculitis with a rise in serum creatinine, dysmorphic hematuria, and red blood cell casts. Because this represents recurrence of active vasculitis threatening kidney function after prior remission, it meets the CYCAZAREM definition of a major relapse.
Importantly, only 1 qualifying vital-organ-threatening BVAS item was required for major relapse. Multiple manifestations were not necessary.

There is no evidence that these manifestations threaten the function of a vital organ. Therefore, the episode meets the CYCAZAREM definition of minor relapse.

A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 24 glomeruli, with segmental fibrinoid necrosis involving 7 glomeruli and cellular crescents involving 8 glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
She receives cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids for induction therapy and subsequently achieves remission. At the start of maintenance therapy, she continues prednisolone according to the IMPROVE protocol. She remains in remission without evidence of recurrent renal or extrarenal vasculitis.
After she has completed 13 months of maintenance therapy, her nephrologist reviews the protocolized glucocorticoid taper.
According to the IMPROVE protocol, what daily dose of prednisolone should she be receiving at this time?
A. Prednisolone should already have been withdrawn
B. 7.5 mg/day
C. 10 mg/day
D. 15 mg/day
E. 5 mg/day
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. 5 mg/day
PART C — Explanation
E is correct. In IMPROVE, prednisolone was reduced to 15 mg/day at the start of the maintenance regimen. It was then tapered to 5 mg/day after 12 months and withdrawn after 24 months. 
This patient has completed 13 months of maintenance therapy. She has therefore passed the 12-month dose-reduction point but has not yet reached the 24-month withdrawal point.
The protocolized sequence is:
Start of maintenance: 15 mg/day
After 12 months: 5 mg/day
After 24 months: withdrawn
Therefore, at month 13 of maintenance therapy, the appropriate prednisolone dose is 5 mg/day.

title: Q196 · Which of the following best describes the applicability of the IMPROVE trial findings to this patient?
body: A 43-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of progressive fatigue, reduced appetite, unintentional weight loss, diffuse myalgia, palpable purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. H
full:
A 43-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of progressive fatigue, reduced appetite, unintentional weight loss, diffuse myalgia, palpable purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. He has a remote history of intravenous drug use. His medical history also includes chronic hepatitis B infection and HIV infection for which he is receiving antiretroviral therapy. His blood pressure is 154/92 mmHg, heart rate is 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, temperature is 37.2 C, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.
MPO-ANCA testing is positive, and he is diagnosed with newly diagnosed microscopic polyangiitis with ANCA-associated vasculitis.
At diagnosis, serum creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL compared with 1.0 mg/dL 7 weeks earlier. Estimated glomerular filtration rate is 33 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with more than 50 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. Estimated proteinuria is 1.7 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 24 glomeruli, with segmental fibrinoid necrosis involving 7 glomeruli and cellular crescents involving 9 glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
He receives cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids for induction therapy and subsequently achieves remission. His nephrologist reviews the IMPROVE trial when considering whether the trial's findings regarding mycophenolate mofetil and azathioprine maintenance therapy can be directly applied to this patient.
Which of the following best describes the applicability of the IMPROVE trial findings to this patient?
A. The findings are not strongly applicable because microscopic polyangiitis was not included among the diagnoses studied in IMPROVE
B. The findings are strongly applicable because newly diagnosed microscopic polyangiitis and positive MPO-ANCA were sufficient for enrollment regardless of chronic infection
C. The findings are strongly applicable because hepatitis B and HIV affected only induction therapy and did not influence eligibility for maintenance randomization
D. The findings are not strongly applicable because IMPROVE excluded all patients with renal involvement at diagnosis
E. The findings are not strongly applicable because patients with hepatitis B infection or positive HIV testing were excluded from IMPROVE
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: E. The findings are not strongly applicable because patients with hepatitis B infection or positive HIV testing were excluded from IMPROVE
PART C — Explanation
E is correct. IMPROVE enrolled patients with newly diagnosed granulomatosis with polyangiitis or microscopic polyangiitis who were 18 to 75 years old and had positive ANCA testing. However, the exclusion criteria included the presence of hepatitis B or C infection and positive testing for HIV, along with several other conditions.
This patient otherwise resembles the studied population because he has newly diagnosed, ANCA-positive microscopic polyangiitis and has achieved remission following induction therapy. However, he also has chronic hepatitis B infection and HIV infection. Both characteristics correspond to explicit IMPROVE exclusion criteria.
Therefore, he is not well represented by the IMPROVE population, and the trial's comparative maintenance findings cannot be considered strongly or directly applicable to his situation.
Importantly, this does not establish that azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil is contraindicated or ineffective in such a patient. It means that IMPROVE did not directly study patients with these infections.

title: Q197 · Which of the following induction approaches is most consistent with the IMPROVE protocol for a patient with severe disease?

full:
A 46-year-old woman presents with a 4-week history of progressive fatigue, reduced appetite, unintentional weight loss, diffuse myalgia, palpable purpura over both lower limbs, dark-colored urine, and worsening shortness of breath. Over the preceding 48 hours, she has developed hemoptysis. Her blood pressure is 158/92 mmHg, heart rate is 102 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute, temperature is 37.4 C, and oxygen saturation is 89% on room air. MPO-ANCA testing is positive, and she is diagnosed with newly diagnosed microscopic polyangiitis with ANCA-associated vasculitis.
Serum creatinine is 3.0 mg/dL compared with 0.9 mg/dL 6 weeks earlier. Estimated glomerular filtration rate is 19 mL/min/1.73 m2. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL compared with 11.7 g/dL 2 weeks earlier.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with more than 50 red blood cells per high-power field, numerous dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. Estimated proteinuria is 1.9 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 25 glomeruli, with segmental fibrinoid necrosis involving 9 glomeruli and cellular crescents involving 11 glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
Chest imaging demonstrates bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, and the clinical findings are attributed to active pulmonary and renal vasculitis. The treating nephrologist reviews the induction regimen permitted in the IMPROVE trial before proceeding to maintenance therapy if remission is achieved.
Which of the following induction approaches is most consistent with the IMPROVE protocol for a patient with severe disease?
A. Mycophenolate mofetil plus glucocorticoids, with plasma exchange and/or up to 3000 mg of methylprednisolone over 3 days permitted
B. Cyclophosphamide plus glucocorticoids, with plasma exchange and/or up to 3000 mg of methylprednisolone over 3 days permitted
C. Azathioprine plus glucocorticoids, with plasma exchange and/or up to 3000 mg of methylprednisolone over 3 days permitted
D. Cyclophosphamide plus glucocorticoids, with neither plasma exchange nor intravenous methylprednisolone permitted during induction
E. Mycophenolate mofetil plus azathioprine, with plasma exchange permitted but glucocorticoids omitted during induction
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: B. Cyclophosphamide plus glucocorticoids, with plasma exchange and/or up to 3000 mg of methylprednisolone over 3 days permitted
PART C — Explanation
B is correct. In IMPROVE, all patients received cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids for induction of remission. In patients with severe disease, the protocol permitted plasma exchange and/or up to a total of 3000 mg of methylprednisolone over 3 days. Cyclophosphamide could be administered either as daily oral therapy or as intermittent intravenous doses for a maximum of 6 months. 
Thus, the IMPROVE induction framework was:
Cyclophosphamide + glucocorticoids
with, for severe disease:
Plasma exchange and/or up to 3000 mg methylprednisolone over 3 days.
Importantly, these additional therapies were permitted rather than mandated for every patient with severe disease.

title: Q198 · According to the IMPROVE trial definitions, how should this event be classified?

full:
A 52-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of progressive fatigue, reduced appetite, unintentional weight loss, diffuse myalgia, palpable purpura over both lower limbs, nasal crusting, and dark-colored urine. His blood pressure is 152/88 mmHg, heart rate is 86 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, temperature is 37.2 C, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. PR3-ANCA testing is positive, and he is diagnosed with newly diagnosed granulomatosis with polyangiitis with ANCA-associated vasculitis.
At diagnosis, serum creatinine is 2.1 mg/dL compared with 0.9 mg/dL 7 weeks earlier. Estimated glomerular filtration rate is 36 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with more than 50 red blood cells per high-power field, numerous dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. Estimated proteinuria is 1.5 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 24 glomeruli, with segmental fibrinoid necrosis involving 6 glomeruli and cellular crescents involving 8 glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
He receives cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids for induction therapy and subsequently achieves remission. He then begins maintenance therapy according to the IMPROVE protocol. His serum creatinine stabilizes at 1.1 mg/dL, the palpable purpura and nasal symptoms resolve, and urinalysis no longer demonstrates red blood cell casts.
At month 18, he develops recurrent fatigue, lower-limb edema, and dark-colored urine. Serum creatinine has increased from 1.1 mg/dL to 2.6 mg/dL. Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood, more than 50 red blood cells per high-power field, numerous dysmorphic red blood cells, and recurrent red blood cell casts. The nephrologist determines that these findings represent new active glomerulonephritis attributable to recurrent vasculitis.
According to the IMPROVE trial definitions, how should this event be classified?
A. Minor relapse
B. Major relapse
C. Persistent disease without relapse
D. Continued remission with residual renal damage
E. Primary failure of induction therapy
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: B. Major relapse
PART C — Explanation
B is correct. IMPROVE defined major relapse as the new appearance of major organ involvement attributable to active vasculitis.
This patient had previously achieved remission, with improvement of renal function and disappearance of active urinary sediment. At month 18, he develops a substantial rise in serum creatinine together with recurrent dysmorphic hematuria and red blood cell casts, and these abnormalities are specifically attributed to new active glomerulonephritis from recurrent vasculitis.
Because this represents new major-organ involvement attributable to active vasculitis after remission, the event meets the IMPROVE definition of a major relapse.

title: Q199 · According to the IMPROVE trial definitions, how should the month-15 event be classified?

According to the IMPROVE trial definitions, how should the month-15 event be classified?
A. Minor relapse
B. Major relapse
C. Persistent disease without relapse
D. Continued remission with residual symptoms
E. Primary failure of induction therapy

Correct Answer: A. Minor relapse
PART C — Explanation
A is correct. IMPROVE defined minor relapse as the recurrence or new occurrence of less severe disease attributable to active vasculitis.
This patient achieved remission at month 3, with resolution of her initial systemic, renal, and upper-airway manifestations. At month 15, she develops recurrent nasal crusting and arthralgia, both attributed to active vasculitis.
Her renal function remains stable, urinalysis shows no evidence of recurrent active glomerulonephritis, and there is no new major-organ involvement.
Therefore, the episode meets the IMPROVE definition of minor relapse.

title: Q200 · According to the IMPROVE trial protocol, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in his trial treatment and follow-up schedule?
body: A 54-year-old man presents with a 7-week history of progressive fatigue, reduced appetite, unintentional weight loss, diffuse myalgia, palpable purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. H
full:

Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
He begins induction therapy with cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids according to the IMPROVE protocol. His renal function and systemic manifestations gradually improve over the following months.
After completing 3 months of induction therapy, his serum creatinine has decreased to 1.5 mg/dL, and estimated glomerular filtration rate has improved to 52 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis now demonstrates 1+ blood, 1+ protein, 8–12 red blood cells per high-power field, and occasional dysmorphic red blood cells, without red blood cell casts. Estimated proteinuria has decreased to 0.6 g/day. His palpable purpura has resolved, but he continues to experience intermittent inflammatory arthralgia and mild nasal crusting attributable to active vasculitis. His Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score is 2.
According to the IMPROVE trial protocol, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in his trial treatment and follow-up schedule?
A. Continue induction therapy through month 9, with follow-up extended to 51 months
B. Continue induction therapy through month 6, with follow-up maintained at 48 months
C. Discontinue induction therapy at month 3, with follow-up extended to 51 months
D. Continue induction therapy through month 6, with follow-up extended to 51 months
E. Discontinue induction therapy at month 3, with follow-up maintained at 48 months
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: D. Continue induction therapy through month 6, with follow-up extended to 51 months
PART C — Explanation
D is correct. According to the IMPROVE protocol, patients who had not achieved remission by 3 months underwent an extension of the induction period to 6 months, with the follow-up period extended to 51 months.
IMPROVE defined remission as a Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score of 0, indicating no new or worsened disease activity or persistently active disease manifestations within the preceding 28 days.
Although this patient demonstrates substantial improvement in renal function, urinary abnormalities, and systemic manifestations, he continues to have clinical manifestations attributed to active vasculitis. His Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score remains 2.
Therefore, he has not achieved remission after completing 3 months of induction therapy.
The IMPROVE protocol specifies extension of induction therapy through month 6 and corresponding extension of follow-up to 51 months.

title: Q201 · According to the primary efficacy findings of the IMPROVE trial, which of the following conclusions is best supported?
body: A 51-year-old man presents with a 7-week history of progressive fatigue, reduced appetite, unintentional weight loss, diffuse myalgia, recurrent epistaxis, nasal crusting, palpable purpura over both l
full:
A 51-year-old man presents with a 7-week history of progressive fatigue, reduced appetite, unintentional weight loss, diffuse myalgia, recurrent epistaxis, nasal crusting, palpable purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. His blood pressure is 154/92 mmHg, heart rate is 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, temperature is 37.2°C, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. PR3-ANCA testing is positive, and he is diagnosed with newly diagnosed granulomatosis with polyangiitis with ANCA-associated vasculitis.
At diagnosis, serum creatinine is 2.6 mg/dL compared with 0.9 mg/dL 8 weeks earlier. Estimated glomerular filtration rate is 27 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with more than 50 red blood cells per high-power field, numerous dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. Estimated proteinuria is 1.7 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 25 glomeruli, with segmental fibrinoid necrosis involving 7 glomeruli and cellular crescents involving 9 glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
He receives cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids for induction therapy. After completing 3 months of treatment, his constitutional symptoms, palpable purpura, nasal crusting, and epistaxis have resolved. Serum creatinine has improved to 1.2 mg/dL, estimated glomerular filtration rate is 68 mL/min/1.73 m2, and urinalysis demonstrates no dysmorphic red blood cells or red blood cell casts. His Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score is 0, and he has no persistently active disease manifestations during the preceding month.
The patient is considered to have achieved remission and is being evaluated for long-term maintenance therapy. His complete blood cell count and liver function tests are within normal limits. He has no history of intolerance to either azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil.
The treating nephrologist reviews the IMPROVE trial to determine which maintenance treatment has stronger evidence for preventing disease relapse.
According to the primary efficacy findings of the IMPROVE trial, which of the following conclusions is best supported?
A. Mycophenolate mofetil is preferred because it was associated with a significantly lower hazard of relapse than azathioprine.
B. Azathioprine is preferred because it was associated with a significantly lower hazard of relapse than mycophenolate mofetil.
C. Either treatment is equally supported because the trial established equivalent efficacy for preventing disease relapse.
D. Mycophenolate mofetil is preferred in patients with renal involvement because it demonstrated superior relapse prevention in this subgroup.
E. Neither treatment is preferred because the trial did not establish a statistically significant difference in overall relapse prevention.
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: B. Azathioprine is preferred because it was associated with a significantly lower hazard of relapse than mycophenolate mofetil.
PART C — Explanation
B is correct. The IMPROVE trial compared mycophenolate mofetil with azathioprine for maintenance of remission in patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis who had achieved remission following induction therapy with cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids.
Relapses occurred significantly more frequently among patients receiving mycophenolate mofetil than among those receiving azathioprine.
The primary efficacy findings were:
Mycophenolate mofetil: 42 of 76 patients experienced relapse (55.3%).
Azathioprine: 30 of 80 patients experienced relapse (37.5%).
Unadjusted hazard ratio for mycophenolate mofetil versus azathioprine: 1.69 (95% CI, 1.06–2.70; P=.03).
Adjusted hazard ratio: 1.80 (95% CI, 1.10–2.93; P=.02).
The unadjusted hazard ratio of 1.69 indicates that patients allocated to mycophenolate mofetil experienced an estimated 69% higher hazard of relapse compared with those allocated to azathioprine.
The result was statistically significant because the 95% confidence interval excluded 1.0 and the P value was below .05.
The difference remained statistically significant after adjustment for the prespecified factors of age, sex, diagnostic subtype, route of cyclophosphamide administration during induction, and baseline serum creatinine.
Therefore, azathioprine demonstrated superior efficacy to mycophenolate mofetil for preventing disease relapse in the IMPROVE study population.

title: Q202 · According to the IMPROVE trial findings, which of the following conclusions regarding major relapse prevention is best supported?
body: A 56-year-old man presents with a 7-week history of progressive fatigue, reduced appetite, unintentional weight loss, diffuse myalgia, palpable purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. H
full:
A 56-year-old man presents with a 7-week history of progressive fatigue, reduced appetite, unintentional weight loss, diffuse myalgia, palpable purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. His blood pressure is 158/94 mmHg, heart rate is 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, temperature is 37.3°C, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. MPO-ANCA testing is positive, and he is diagnosed with newly diagnosed microscopic polyangiitis with ANCA-associated vasculitis.
At diagnosis, serum creatinine is 3.2 mg/dL compared with 1.0 mg/dL 8 weeks earlier. Estimated glomerular filtration rate is 20 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with more than 50 red blood cells per high-power field, numerous dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. Estimated proteinuria is 2.1 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 26 glomeruli, with segmental fibrinoid necrosis involving 9 glomeruli and cellular crescents involving 11 glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
He receives cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids for induction therapy. After completing 3 months of treatment, his constitutional symptoms and palpable purpura have resolved. Serum creatinine has improved to 1.4 mg/dL, estimated glomerular filtration rate is 57 mL/min/1.73 m2, and urinalysis demonstrates no dysmorphic red blood cells or red blood cell casts. His Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score is 0, with no persistently active disease manifestations during the preceding 28 days.
The patient subsequently begins maintenance therapy. Given the severity of his initial renal involvement, his nephrologist is particularly concerned about the prevention of major relapses that could result in further organ damage.
The nephrologist reviews the IMPROVE trial, which compared mycophenolate mofetil with azathioprine for remission maintenance in ANCA-associated vasculitis, focusing specifically on the occurrence of major relapses.
According to the IMPROVE trial findings, which of the following conclusions regarding major relapse prevention is best supported?
A. Major relapses were more frequent with azathioprine, but the difference was not statistically significant.
B. Major relapses were more frequent with mycophenolate mofetil, but the difference was not statistically significant.
C. Major relapses were more frequent with mycophenolate mofetil, and the difference was statistically significant.
D. Major relapse rates were comparable, establishing equivalent efficacy between the two maintenance treatments.
E. Major relapses were more frequent with azathioprine, and the difference was statistically significant.
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: B. Major relapses were more frequent with mycophenolate mofetil, but the difference was not statistically significant.
PART C — Explanation
B is correct. In the IMPROVE trial, major relapses occurred numerically more frequently among patients receiving mycophenolate mofetil than among those receiving azathioprine.
The major-relapse findings were:
Mycophenolate mofetil: 18 major relapses among 76 patients (23.7%).
Azathioprine: 10 major relapses among 80 patients (12.5%).
Unadjusted hazard ratio for major relapse with mycophenolate mofetil versus azathioprine: 2.14.
95% confidence interval: 0.99–4.64.
P=.054.
The hazard ratio of 2.14 indicates that patients allocated to mycophenolate mofetil had an estimated 2.14-fold hazard of major relapse compared with those allocated to azathioprine.
However, the difference did not reach the conventional threshold for statistical significance.
The P value of .054 exceeds .05, and the 95% confidence interval includes 1.0. Therefore, although the point estimate favors azathioprine, the study did not establish a statistically significant difference between the groups for major relapse.
Importantly, the absence of statistical significance does not demonstrate that the treatments are equivalent. The confidence interval is wide, reflecting uncertainty regarding the magnitude of the treatment effect.
This finding must also be distinguished from the trial's overall relapse results.
For overall relapses, including both major and minor relapses, the IMPROVE trial demonstrated a statistically significant increase in relapse hazard with mycophenolate mofetil:
Unadjusted HR: 1.69 (95% CI, 1.06–2.70; P=.03).
Adjusted HR: 1.80 (95% CI, 1.10–2.93; P=.02).
Thus, IMPROVE demonstrated significantly better overall relapse prevention with azathioprine, but its separate major-relapse analysis did not establish a statistically significant between-group difference.

B. Mycophenolate mofetil was associated with significantly higher hazards of both overall relapse and major relapse compared with azathioprine.

D. Azathioprine was associated with a significantly higher hazard of overall relapse, while major relapse did not differ significantly between groups.

PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: A. Mycophenolate mofetil was associated with a significantly higher hazard of overall relapse, while its higher hazard of major relapse did not reach statistical significance.
PART C — Explanation
A is correct. The IMPROVE trial demonstrated a statistically significant increase in the hazard of overall relapse among patients receiving mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) compared with azathioprine (AZA). Overall relapse findings:
MMF: 42 of 76 patients experienced relapse (55.3%).
AZA: 30 of 80 patients experienced relapse (37.5%).

MMF: 18 major relapses among 76 patients (23.7%).
AZA: 10 major relapses among 80 patients (12.5%).
Unadjusted HR: 2.14 (95% CI, 0.99–4.64; P=.054).

Therefore, IMPROVE did not demonstrate a statistically significant difference in major relapse between the treatment groups.
Importantly, a nonsignificant result does not establish equivalent efficacy. The major-relapse estimate remains compatible with a range of treatment effects, including a potentially substantial increase in hazard with MMF.

title: Q204 · According to the IMPROVE trial findings, which of the following conclusions is best supported?
body: A 54-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of progressive fatigue, reduced appetite, unintentional weight loss, diffuse myalgia, palpable purpura over both lower limbs, recurrent epistaxis, nasa
full:
A 54-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of progressive fatigue, reduced appetite, unintentional weight loss, diffuse myalgia, palpable purpura over both lower limbs, recurrent epistaxis, nasal crusting, and dark-colored urine. His blood pressure is 154/92 mmHg, heart rate is 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, temperature is 37.2°C, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. PR3-ANCA testing is positive, and he is diagnosed with newly diagnosed granulomatosis with polyangiitis with ANCA-associated vasculitis.
At diagnosis, serum creatinine is 2.7 mg/dL compared with 1.0 mg/dL 8 weeks earlier. Estimated glomerular filtration rate is 26 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with more than 50 red blood cells per high-power field, numerous dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. Estimated proteinuria is 1.8 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 25 glomeruli, with segmental fibrinoid necrosis involving 8 glomeruli and cellular crescents involving 10 glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
He receives cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids for induction therapy. After completing 3 months of treatment, his constitutional symptoms, palpable purpura, epistaxis, and nasal crusting have resolved. Serum creatinine has improved to 1.3 mg/dL, estimated glomerular filtration rate is 61 mL/min/1.73 m2, and urinalysis demonstrates no dysmorphic red blood cells or red blood cell casts. His Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score is 0, with no persistently active disease manifestations during the preceding 28 days.
The patient is considered to have achieved remission and is being evaluated for maintenance therapy. His complete blood cell count and liver function tests are within normal limits. He has no previous history of severe infections, cytopenias, or intolerance to either azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil.
The treating nephrologist reviews the IMPROVE trial to compare the efficacy and safety of azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil for remission maintenance, particularly their effects on disease relapse and severe adverse events.
According to the IMPROVE trial findings, which of the following conclusions is best supported?
A. Azathioprine demonstrated superior relapse prevention, but was associated with a significantly higher risk of severe adverse events than mycophenolate mofetil.
B. Mycophenolate mofetil demonstrated superior relapse prevention, without a statistically significant difference in severe adverse-event risk compared with azathioprine.
C. Mycophenolate mofetil demonstrated superior relapse prevention and a significantly lower risk of severe adverse events compared with azathioprine.
D. Azathioprine demonstrated superior relapse prevention, without a statistically significant difference in severe adverse-event risk compared with mycophenolate mofetil.
E. Neither treatment demonstrated superior relapse prevention, and the risk of severe adverse events was not statistically different between the groups.
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: D. Azathioprine demonstrated superior relapse prevention, without a statistically significant difference in severe adverse-event risk compared with mycophenolate mofetil.
PART C — Explanation
D is correct. The IMPROVE trial demonstrated that azathioprine was more effective than mycophenolate mofetil at preventing disease relapse in patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis who had achieved remission following induction therapy.
However, although severe adverse events were numerically more frequent in the azathioprine group, the trial did not demonstrate a statistically significant difference in severe adverse-event risk between the two maintenance treatments.
Overall relapse findings:
Mycophenolate mofetil: 42 of 76 patients experienced relapse (55.3%).
Azathioprine: 30 of 80 patients experienced relapse (37.5%).
Unadjusted HR for mycophenolate mofetil versus azathioprine: 1.69 (95% CI, 1.06–2.70; P=.03).
Adjusted HR: 1.80 (95% CI, 1.10–2.93; P=.02).
The unadjusted hazard ratio of 1.69 indicates an estimated 69% higher hazard of overall relapse among patients allocated to mycophenolate mofetil compared with those allocated to azathioprine.
The difference was statistically significant because the 95% confidence interval excluded 1.0 and the P value was below .05.
The increased relapse hazard associated with mycophenolate mofetil remained statistically significant after adjustment for age, sex, diagnostic subtype, route of cyclophosphamide administration during induction, and baseline serum creatinine.
Therefore, azathioprine demonstrated superior efficacy for preventing overall disease relapse.
Severe adverse-event findings:
Azathioprine: 22 severe adverse events occurred among 13 patients.
Mycophenolate mofetil: 8 severe adverse events occurred among 8 patients.
HR for mycophenolate mofetil versus azathioprine: 0.53 (95% CI, 0.23–1.18; P=.12).
Although the point estimate suggests a lower hazard of severe adverse events with mycophenolate mofetil, the difference was not statistically significant.
The 95% confidence interval includes 1.0, and the P value exceeds .05.
Consequently, IMPROVE did not establish that mycophenolate mofetil was significantly safer than azathioprine with respect to severe adverse events.
The number of severe adverse events also differs from the number of patients experiencing them because individual patients could experience more than one event. Therefore, the event counts must not be interpreted as the number of affected patients.
The appropriate interpretation is that azathioprine demonstrated significantly better overall relapse prevention, while no statistically significant difference in severe adverse-event risk was established.

title: Q205 · According to the IMPROVE trial findings, which of the following conclusions regarding severe infection risk is best supported?
body: A 55-year-old man presents with a 7-week history of progressive fatigue, reduced appetite, unintentional weight loss, diffuse myalgia, palpable purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. H
full:
A 55-year-old man presents with a 7-week history of progressive fatigue, reduced appetite, unintentional weight loss, diffuse myalgia, palpable purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. His blood pressure is 154/92 mmHg, heart rate is 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, temperature is 37.2°C, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. MPO-ANCA testing is positive, and he is diagnosed with newly diagnosed microscopic polyangiitis with ANCA-associated vasculitis.
At diagnosis, serum creatinine is 2.9 mg/dL compared with 1.0 mg/dL 8 weeks earlier. Estimated glomerular filtration rate is 23 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with more than 50 red blood cells per high-power field, numerous dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. Estimated proteinuria is 1.9 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 26 glomeruli, with segmental fibrinoid necrosis involving 8 glomeruli and cellular crescents involving 10 glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
His medical history is notable for recurrent episodes of bacterial sinusitis and two episodes of community-acquired pneumonia during the preceding 3 years, both of which resolved following antibiotic treatment. He has no evidence of active infection at the time of his vasculitis diagnosis.
He receives cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids for induction therapy. After completing 3 months of treatment, his constitutional symptoms and palpable purpura have resolved. Serum creatinine has improved to 1.3 mg/dL, estimated glomerular filtration rate is 61 mL/min/1.73 m2, and urinalysis demonstrates no dysmorphic red blood cells or red blood cell casts. His Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score is 0, with no persistently active disease manifestations during the preceding 28 days.
The patient subsequently becomes eligible for maintenance therapy. His complete blood cell count and liver function tests are within normal limits. Given his history of recurrent respiratory infections, the treating nephrologist is particularly concerned about the comparative risk of severe infections associated with azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil.
The nephrologist reviews the IMPROVE trial to determine whether one maintenance treatment demonstrated a lower risk of severe infections.
According to the IMPROVE trial findings, which of the following conclusions regarding severe infection risk is best supported?
A. Severe infections were numerically more frequent with azathioprine, but the difference was not statistically significant.
B. Mycophenolate mofetil demonstrated a significantly lower risk of severe infections than azathioprine.
C. Severe infections were numerically more frequent with mycophenolate mofetil, but the difference was not statistically significant.
D. Azathioprine demonstrated a significantly lower risk of severe infections than mycophenolate mofetil.
E. The treatments demonstrated equivalent severe infection risks, establishing comparable safety for this outcome.
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: A. Severe infections were numerically more frequent with azathioprine, but the difference was not statistically significant.
PART C — Explanation
A is correct. In the IMPROVE trial, severe infections occurred numerically more frequently among patients receiving azathioprine than among those receiving mycophenolate mofetil. However, the difference did not reach statistical significance.
The severe infection findings were:
Azathioprine: 8 severe infections among 8 patients.
Mycophenolate mofetil: 3 severe infections among 3 patients.
Hazard ratio for mycophenolate mofetil versus azathioprine: 0.52.
95% confidence interval: 0.11–2.36.
P=.40.
The hazard ratio of 0.52 indicates that the estimated hazard of severe infection was lower in the mycophenolate mofetil group compared with the azathioprine group.
However, the 95% confidence interval includes 1.0, and the P value of .40 exceeds the conventional statistical significance threshold of .05.
Therefore, IMPROVE did not demonstrate a statistically significant difference in severe infection risk between the two maintenance treatments.
The wide confidence interval indicates considerable uncertainty regarding the magnitude and direction of the treatment effect. The findings are compatible with a lower or potentially higher hazard of severe infection with mycophenolate mofetil.
Consequently, the numerically lower number of severe infections in the mycophenolate mofetil group does not establish that it is a safer maintenance treatment with respect to severe infections.
For this patient, the history of recurrent respiratory infections raises an important clinical concern when selecting immunosuppressive maintenance therapy. However, the IMPROVE results do not establish that mycophenolate mofetil provides a statistically significant reduction in severe infection risk compared with azathioprine.
The trial also demonstrated a statistically significant difference in overall relapse prevention favoring azathioprine, with an unadjusted hazard ratio of 1.69 for mycophenolate mofetil versus azathioprine (95% CI, 1.06–2.70; P=.03).
Therefore, the comparative infection findings must be interpreted separately from the established difference in relapse prevention.

title: Q206 · According to the IMPROVE trial findings, which of the following conclusions regarding renal outcomes is best supported?
body: A 55-year-old man presents with a 7-week history of progressive fatigue, reduced appetite, unintentional weight loss, diffuse myalgia, palpable purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. H
full:
A 55-year-old man presents with a 7-week history of progressive fatigue, reduced appetite, unintentional weight loss, diffuse myalgia, palpable purpura over both lower limbs, and dark-colored urine. His blood pressure is 156/94 mmHg, heart rate is 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, temperature is 37.2°C, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. MPO-ANCA testing is positive, and he is diagnosed with newly diagnosed microscopic polyangiitis with ANCA-associated vasculitis.
At diagnosis, serum creatinine is 3.1 mg/dL compared with 1.0 mg/dL 8 weeks earlier. Estimated glomerular filtration rate is 22 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with more than 50 red blood cells per high-power field, numerous dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. Estimated proteinuria is 2.1 g/day.
A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 26 glomeruli, with segmental fibrinoid necrosis involving 9 glomeruli and cellular crescents involving 11 glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits.
He receives cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids for induction therapy. After completing 3 months of treatment, his constitutional symptoms and palpable purpura have resolved. Serum creatinine has improved to 1.6 mg/dL, estimated glomerular filtration rate is 48 mL/min/1.73 m2, and urinalysis demonstrates no dysmorphic red blood cells or red blood cell casts. Estimated proteinuria has decreased to 0.8 g/day. His Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score is 0, with no persistently active disease manifestations during the preceding 28 days.
Although he has achieved remission, he continues to have reduced kidney function and residual proteinuria, attributed to chronic kidney damage from his previous renal vasculitis. He is subsequently evaluated for maintenance therapy with either azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil.
The treating nephrologist reviews the IMPROVE trial to determine whether either maintenance treatment demonstrated superior preservation of renal function or greater improvement in proteinuria during follow-up.
According to the IMPROVE trial findings, which of the following conclusions regarding renal outcomes is best supported?
A. Azathioprine demonstrated significantly better eGFR outcomes, while proteinuria reduction did not differ significantly between treatments.
B. Mycophenolate mofetil demonstrated significantly greater proteinuria reduction, while eGFR outcomes did not differ significantly between treatments.
C. Azathioprine demonstrated significantly better eGFR outcomes, while mycophenolate mofetil demonstrated significantly greater proteinuria reduction.
D. Neither treatment demonstrated a statistically significant advantage in eGFR or proteinuria outcomes during follow-up.
E. Mycophenolate mofetil demonstrated significantly better eGFR outcomes and greater proteinuria reduction compared with azathioprine.
PART B — Correct Answer
Correct Answer: D. Neither treatment demonstrated a statistically significant advantage in eGFR or proteinuria outcomes during follow-up.
PART C — Explanation
D is correct. The IMPROVE trial compared mycophenolate mofetil with azathioprine for remission maintenance in patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis who had achieved remission following induction therapy with cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids.
Although azathioprine demonstrated superior efficacy in preventing overall disease relapse, the trial did not demonstrate statistically significant between-group differences in estimated glomerular filtration rate or proteinuria outcomes.
Estimated glomerular filtration rate findings:
At the end of the study, median estimated glomerular filtration rates were:
Mycophenolate mofetil: 52.8 mL/min/1.73 m2 (IQR, 38.5–70.1).
Azathioprine: 59.2 mL/min/1.73 m2 (IQR, 45.2–71.7).
P=.35.
Although the median eGFR was numerically higher in the azathioprine group, the difference was not statistically significant.
Therefore, IMPROVE did not establish that azathioprine provided superior preservation of kidney function compared with mycophenolate mofetil.
Proteinuria findings:
The median reduction in proteinuria over the study was:
Mycophenolate mofetil: 0.82 g/day.
Azathioprine: 0.53 g/day.
P=.26.
Although the median reduction in proteinuria was numerically greater in the mycophenolate mofetil group, this difference was not statistically significant.
Therefore, IMPROVE did not establish that mycophenolate mofetil produced a superior reduction in proteinuria compared with azathioprine.
These findings must be distinguished from the trial's primary efficacy outcome.
Overall relapses occurred in 42 of 76 patients receiving mycophenolate mofetil compared with 30 of 80 patients receiving azathioprine.
The unadjusted hazard ratio for overall relapse with mycophenolate mofetil versus azathioprine was 1.69 (95% CI, 1.06–2.70; P=.03).
Thus, azathioprine demonstrated statistically significantly better overall relapse prevention, but this did not translate into a demonstrated statistically significant advantage in eGFR or proteinuria outcomes during the study.
Importantly, the absence of statistically significant differences in renal outcomes does not establish that the treatments are equivalent in their effects on kidney function or proteinuria.

title: Q207 · According to the investigators' conclusions from the IMPROVE trial, which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation when selecting initial maintenance therapy for this patient?
body: A 52-year-old man presents with a 7-week history of progressive fatigue, reduced appetite, unintentional weight loss, diffuse myalgia, recurrent epistaxis, nasal crusting, palpable purpura over both l
full:
